speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I trust hon. members will allow me to make a few brief remarks on the tragedy we are commemorating today.

Today marks the fiftieth anniversary of the destruction by fire of the original parliament buildings of Canada. The blaze broke out in the reading room at 8.55 p.m. and spread swiftly throughout the building. At the time the house was debating problems concerning the fishing industry.
Hon. members may be interested in the following extract from Hansard of February 3, 1916, as reported at page 578:
9 p.m.
At this time Mr. C. R. Stewart, Chief Doorkeeper of the House of Commons, came hurriedly into the Chamber and called out: "There is a big fire in the reading room; everybody get out quickly." The sitting was immediately suspended without formality, and members, officials, and visitors in the galleries, fled from the Chamber. Some of them were almost overcome by the rapidly-advancing smoke and flames before reaching a place of safety. The fire, which had originated in the reading room, gained momentum with extreme rapidity and was soon beyond control. It continued till the following day, resulting in the almost total destruction of the parliament buildings, together with the loss of several lives.
As hon. members know, the only part of the original building remaining virtually intact was the library. Following the disaster, parliament met in the lecture theatre of the Victoria Memorial Museum and sessions continued there until February 2, 1920, when parliament met in the present building for the first time. Yesterday marked our 46th year in this chamber of our parliament.
Among the casualties of the fire was the mace. A temporary replacement was hastily constructed and was used for several months after the fire, and it is this mace which is in use today.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will make a statement with regard to Rhodesia and the government's intentions respecting further measures.
Members of the house will recall that on November 11, immediately after the unilateral and illegal declaration of independence by the Smith regime in Rhodesia, the Prime Minister announced that the Canadian government did not recognize this declaration, the allegedly independent state, or the illegal
Supply-External Affairs regime in Rhodesia which had been dismissed from office by the Governor. At the same time we withdrew our trade commissioner from Salisbury and took certain economic measures against Rhodesia, including the ending of our small aid program, a complete arms embargo, and the withdrawal of Commonwealth preferences for Rhodesian goods entering Canada and of our export credit facilities for Canadian goods going to Rhodesia.
Since November 11 the Canadian government has played its full part in efforts to bring to an early end the illegal situation in that country by non-military means. The British government has taken the lead in these efforts in view of its constitutional responsibility for Rhodesia. In addition, we have also based our actions on United Nations resolutions and in particular on the Security Council resolution of November 20 which recommends that member countries should sever their economic relations with the Rhodesian regime.
Acting in close consultation with Britain, our other commonwealth partners and with other countries with significant trade with Rhodesia, we have progressively introduced further trade measures against Rhodesia. Before today these measures involved an embargo on our main imports from Rhodesia accounting for some 98 per cent of our normal imports from that country. I think in answer to the Leader of the Opposition the other day I said something over 90 per cent.
On the export side, in addition to our ban on the export of arms we had placed a total embargo on the export of oil and oil products from Canada to Rhodesia. This measure was mainly precautionary to prevent transshipments or sales in lieu of other suppliers, since we normally do not export oil or oil products to Rhodesia. Our exports were also inhibited by the suspension of export credits and export credit insurance facilities. If account is taken of the sharp curtailment of trade imposed upon Rhodesia by the effect of the sanctions, including its foreign exchange earnings as well as the inhibiting effects of the uncertainties and risks surrounding trade with Rhodesia, the actual impact on our trade with Rhodesia has been to reduce drastically commercial exchanges in both directions.
In keeping with our position at the Lagos conference in January about which the Prime Minister has already reported to the house, and in the light of the new British measures
February 3, 1966

Supply-External Affairs of last Sunday, I am now in a position to inform the house that the Canadian government has decided to consolidate and extend its economic measures against Rhodesia by a total import and export embargo with certain limited exceptions.
What have been the exceptions up to the present?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Would my right hon. friend permit me to finish and then I will give him the exceptions.
Export permit applications will continue to be considered in the case of food, medical supplies, other goods for humanitarian purposes and goods which are for the essential needs of the Rhodesian railways, Central African railways and the Central African Power Corporation which are operated jointly by Zambia and Rhodesia.
These new measures provide tangible evidence of our strong continued support, in concert with our commonwealth partners and others, for the efforts to bring about an early end to the illegal situation in Rhodesia. We remain in close consultation with the British government, the United States and other countries which have joined in the economic sanctions against Rhodesia, and we believe that our action and similar measures by other countries will make a further and significant contribution toward ending the illegal regime in Rhodesia.
I should like to deal now with the question posed a moment ago by the Leader of the Opposition. I deal first with the situation prior to the decision which I have just announced.
Import bans against Rhodesia on sugar, tobacco, ferrochrome, chrome ores and concentrates, asbestos, and preserved meats affect some 98 per cent of traditional Canadian imports from Rhodesia on the basis of trade statistics for 1964, when total Canadian imports from that country amounted to $4.3 million. The remaining commodities not covered under our present import bans, that is, under the import bans as of yesterday, include only small quantities of green beans, lemon and orange oil, electrical equipment, clothing, green peanuts and food product machinery and parts.
In imposing import bans against Rhodesia we have concentrated, as did the British, on the most significant Rhodesian exports. Before the new British measures were announced on Sunday involving a complete

trade embargo against Rhodesia, British import bans against Rhodesia covered some 95 per cent of total British imports.
On the export side, again as before the announcement of today, the bans introduced affected oil and oil products, and arms, ammunition and military equipment. The ban on oil and oil products was essentially, as I said, a precautionary measure since we do not normally export oil to Rhodesia. Total Canadian exports to Rhodesia in 1964 amounted to $3.1 million.

Mr. Chairman, I very much appreciate the statement of the minister on Rhodesia and in a few moments I should like to deal with his remarks and some other aspects of this matter in more detail. In the meanwhile there are one or two matters I should like to bring before the committee for consideration and I shall now proceed with those.
The first matter concerns Her Majesty. You may consider this a rather strange place to bring up the subject of Her Majesty, but since the remarks I have in mind affect other members of the commonwealth I thought this forum the best one perhaps in which to introduce these comments.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
As everyone is aware, the commonwealth is divided into two groups, those countries which recognize Her Majesty as the head of the government and those which are constituted as republics but are nevertheless members of the commonwealth. In addition, there is the state of Malaysia which is a separate, elected monarchy. The countries which recognize the Queen as head of the commonwealth are Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, Trinidad and Tobago, Jamaica, Ceylon, Sierra Leone, Malta, Gambia and Malawi. Those which do not are India, Pakistan, Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana, Cyprus, Singapore, Uganda, Zambia and Nigeria.
If Canada is to continue as a constitutional monarchy, and I wish to make it clear that I certainly think we should, we have to bring ourselves up to date. Though it is true that Her Majesty has made many visits to Canada which have been happy occasions, the fact is that she has almost always been involved in very exhausting royal tours which I believe are an imposition on her, and do not really satisfy the requirements that in my opinion should be fulfilled by a constitutional monarch. We agree that Her Majesty has had
February 3, 1966

excellent representatives in this country. I have in mind particularly the present representative and the previous incumbent of that office, both of them Canadians. These are men of whom we can all be proud. But if we are to continue to have a system of constitutional monarchy in Canada we must be honoured more frequently by the presence of Her Majesty herself.
I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister announce that arrangements were now being made to have Her Majesty visit Canada in our centennial year. Again, if this is to be one of those exhausting trips which can do little save injure the health of Her Majesty while at the same time giving her Canadian subjects little chance to see her or become properly acquainted with her, I question the usefulness of such a visit.
The suggestion I am about to make would not have been possible 50, 25, or perhaps even 10 years ago, but because of the revolution in the field of transport many things are now possible which were not possible in the past. I think we should take advantage of these changes and adjust our political and economic system to the achievements of science. Fifty years ago it would have taken Her Majesty longer to get from London half way to the Scottish border than it would take her today to reach Ottawa by air.
It is my feeling and that of many others in this house that Her Majesty should spend more of her time in her Canadian kingdom. There is no reason why Her Majesty could not at least open every new parliament and be in Canada for a specific period of time each year or at least every other year. I would hope that on those occasions Her Majesty would not be pressed to move about the country on exhausting tours but rather that she would be given the opportunity to make more leisurely visits to various parts of her Canadian realm and meet her subjects in a more informal way under much less pressure than in the past.
I bring this up now because, as I indicated earlier, Her Majesty is also the sovereign of Australia, New Zealand and the other countries I mentioned. These countries might wish to make similar arrangements. Also, since the traditional seat of royalty is in the United Kingdom, these matters might well be the subject of consultation between the members of the commonwealths concerned. We have a Commonwealth Secretariat presided over by
Supply-External Affairs a distinguished Canadian civil servant, Mr. Arnold Smith, of whom we are all proud, and this is a matter which might well be gone into.
Some might say: If Her Majesty takes up residence in Canada, where will she stay? I believe the answer is simple. The government could make an appropriation, perhaps by removing a little from the World Fair allotment if necessary, and build an addition to Rideau Hall to provide Her Majesty with permanent quarters when she comes to Canada. I think it would be a splendid thing to be able to announce in our centenary year that Her Majesty would be Queen of Canada not just by representation but by her presence for a few weeks each year.
The next matter I should like to discuss briefly involves our relations with Latin America. From time to time I hear indications from the government that it is just about but not quite ready to join the Organization of American States. This has been a controversial issue in Canada for a number of years. Many of us have held views both ways on the subject.
I believe it would be most unwise for Canada to join the Organization of American States as that organization is now constituted. If arrangement could be made to change that organization it might be advisable to join but in present circumstances it might be very unwise indeed. If any proof is needed, all one has to do is examine carefully what took place when the crisis arose in the Dominican Republic. Had Canada belonged to the organization on that occasion, our membership would have done no good to our relations with Washington or to our relations with the Latin American countries. We would have been caught in the middle of a squeeze play. It would have done us no good at all. At present we have excellent relations, both diplomatic and commercial, with all countries in Latin America and I can see nothing but trouble for us if we join this organization as it is at present constituted.
I know that many who are associated with foreign affairs in this house as well as senior members of the civil service and other Canadians who interest themselves in these matters have, so to speak, had their arms twisted by interested persons both from the United States and from the Latin American countries. Latin Americans have told me, as I am sure they have told other hon. members: We should like to see Canada in the organization because you can explain our situation to
648	COMMONS
Supply-External Affairs Washington. Similarly, I have heard our United States friends say: We should like to have you in the organization because you can explain our situation to the Latin American countries. My only comment is that when a third party tries to stop an argument between two neighbours hon. members know who usually gets his head battered.
What I should like to see is an expansion and strengthening of our relationships on a bilateral basis with the countries of Latin America, Mexico in particular. Mexico and Canada, as I have pointed out in this house on other occasions, have much in common. We each have a common border with our great neighbour. Mexico has been increasingly one of our better customers commercially. The tourist business, from the Mexican point of view, has been excellent so far as the arrival of Canadians is concerned. There are a number of ways in which we could improve relationships with countries in Latin America. Some are already under consideration by the government and I hope these efforts will come to fruition in the near future.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There is another matter I wish to mention having to do with immigration and which is connected very directly to our relations with Latin America. As everyone knows, there is a great shortage of both skilled and unskilled labour in Canada. No one is more aware of this than the former minister of citizenship and immigration, now the Minister of Labour, and it must also be of concern to the new minister who will be in charge of manpower.
One source of desirable immigration to Canada might well be some of the Latin American countries which have economic problems and where increasing populations are a matter of great concern. Enough fantasy. I want to make some remarks and I ask the minister for his comments in his reply.
I wish to speak about federal and provincial jurisdiction in international matters. This is very much discussed in Canada at the present time, as it will be also in the near future. I was reading in La Presse this afternoon, that on February 5 next, an important symposium will be held at the Laval University faculty of law on the relations between Quebec and foreign countries. Of the papers to be presented, may I mention that of Claude Morin, on the interdepartmental committee, and that of Mr. Sabourin, on Canadian presence abroad.

There, then, is one topic which is very much discussed in Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec. In this connection, Mr. Chairman, we face two alternatives. That of the central government and that put forward for the past 12 to 18 months by Quebec and especially by the Minister of Education and the Minister of Cultural Affairs of the province.
The central government maintains it alone can deal with international matters because of precedents or constitutional principles. The Quebec government, through the two ministers I have mentioned, asserts in great detail and with much conviction that a province can, without the authorization of the central government, establish relations, carry on negotiations and sign treaties in fields which come under its exclusive jurisdiction.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Here is how the Quebec government logically explains its attitude. Any province has the right to do so because it can legislate in matters under its jurisdiction. Therefore, the right of negotiation precedes the right of implementation.
What about the principle behind those two opinions, those two attitudes? In the first place, who has the right to negotiate with foreign countries? According to international law, when international principles are involved, you have to refer to the constitutional law of the country in question, because this concerns the internal legislation of that country. Now, under the Canadian constitutional law, what governments can negotiate treaties in the field of international relations?
Before 1867, the Colonial Office in London was negotiating and signing treaties on behalf of Canada.
From 1867 to 1931, the Canadian constitution was strong and meaningful due to section 132 enabling only the federal government to perform international obligations entered into as part of the empire. For the information of hon. members, I shall quote section 132 which reads as follows:
The parliament and government of Canada shall have all powers necessary or proper for performing the obligations of Canada or of any province thereof, as part of the British empire, toward foreign countries arising under treaties between the empire and such foreign countries.
Therefore this section is clear: only the central government, as part of the empire, could perform obligations.
But in 1931, under the Statute of Westminster, this section lapsed and became ob-
February 3, 1966	COMMONS
solete when our country became a sovereign and independent state, with the various attributes of a sovereign country.
Later, in 1937, the privy council in London ruled in the Labour Convention Case that the central government cannot, in areas of specific provincial jurisdiction, commit the provinces. That decision followed upon certain regulations set up in connection with decisions or rulings of the International Labour Congress.
But section 132 having been obsolete and void since 1931, due to the new constitutional changes in the country, there is no longer any section in our constitution to guide us on this point. On the basis of the wording of sections 92, 93 and 95 of the constitution, it should nevertheless be noted that when the provinces joined to create the central government, in 1867, no apparent provision was made by which the provinces reserved for themselves certain areas of jurisdiction as far as relations, negotiations or the signing of international treaties were concerned.
If Quebec presses with great vigour the argument that I mentioned a while ago, and more particularly in the last couple of years, it is not so much because of its provincial status but rather because of its special status. Quebec, in addition to its ordinary provincial status, is asking for a special status, because it is the national homeland of all French Canadians in Canada and, indeed, in North America. It is under this special social and cultural aspect that the government of Quebec claims a status and responsibilities in the field of international relations.
I cannot see, Mr. Chairman-and I call the minister's attention to this-how it can affect the latitude and the responsibility of the central government to recognize international jurisdiction for the provinces. It seems that some provinces, like Ontario for instance, for a number of years and apparently without any authorization from the central government, without any previous agreement being reached or without any master agreement, have established relations with different countries in the educational, scientific and commercial fields.
If, in Quebec, there is talk of international jurisdiction it follows mostly from the special status of the province. I do not see how it could be harmful to a well-planned and well-implemented Canadian federalism that Quebec should have the right to negotiate treaties with other countries in certain fields

I would be in favour of that. The minister should consider the matter and give us some definite information or his views as to how the question should be approached. English speaking Canadians of various racial origins had the opportunity to travel in South America or elsewhere and told us afterwards about the warm reception they received, especially in South America, and how glad people were to meet them because they came from a country where French is spoken and which has a Latin background, in short, a bicultural country.

Mr. Chairman, I was wondering if the Secretary of State for External Affairs wanted to speak now? I know how trying it is for him to sit silent for such a long period and I do not want to see him suffer. If he wants to speak now I would gladly relinquish my position.
I will let my friend do his suffering for now.

Thank you. I should like the minister to explain how the $155 million in the estimates has been spent during the course of this fiscal year and I am wondering about the supplementary estimate for which he is asking.
Although he has made two speeches on external affairs in the course of the session so far, we are now embarked on a close study of the expenditure of money by his department.


I had thought he would have made some exposition with regard to the $155 million that is listed in the estimates for the fiscal year. Of course, for that amount he has had a blank cheque for a 10 month period. Perhaps he would like to explain how that blank cheque has been used. No doubt we shall hear from him later.
My purpose in speaking today is chiefly to deal with the situation in Viet Nam, although I am very keenly interested in the action which the government has taken with regard to Southern Rhodesia and which it has not indicated fully to the house. I think the hon. member for Oxford was quite correct in saying that this action was a departure from our normal diplomatic relations in the world and that it has set a precedent for the future. The background to the arrangements and the steps that have been taken could have been more clearly set out to parliament. I submit as a matter of fact that parliament should have been called into special session before Christmas to deal with the matter. I doubt very much that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is on sound ground in the action which he has recommended to the government. However, that he will have to explain. We shall give him plenty of time to do so.
I am very much interested in the position of the government with regard to South Viet Nam. In that regard I should like to examine the minister's statements. May I submit that we are faced with this position concerning Southeast Asia. There has been trouble there for 20 years now and it is not going to go away by wishful thinking. This trouble has become of increasing importance within the last year and is rapidly reaching a crisis.
Under the circumstances, what are we to do? I listened very carefully to the minister a week ago when he was setting out Canada's position with regard to that conflict. I have also read with a great deal of interest the statement he made to the External Affairs Committee on June 9 and 10 last in which he gave a comprehensive review of the situation in South Viet Nam and the historical background. Those who are interested in the subject should refer to that. I have credited the document to the Secretary of State for External Affairs but of course his officials had prepared it for him. However, it has been very well done and gives the picture clearly. Where do we go from here? That is the question I have been asking myself ever since listening to the minister.
February 3, 1966

On January 25 he spoke in the house with what I considered to be unusual vigour and determination. He spoke rather clearly too, which was delightful, and we were able to follow him. As I say, I was amazed at the vigour with which he dealt with the subject up to a certain point. I think it is important to recall what he said when he was answering the question which is in the minds of all of us, namely, how important is the struggle in South Viet Nam? This is what he said on page 234 of Hansard:
We must ask ourselves what the failure of United States efforts in Asia would mean to us as well as to that country.
That is a very good question. It is in the minds of a lot of people.
We must ask ourselves what it would mean to India, to Thailand, to the island countries, the Philippines, New Zealand and Australia. We must ask ourselves what it would mean to many countries in Asia and Africa which, although critical of the United States, would be deeply concerned over a Communist victory in Viet Nam. I ask what would be the concern of the Soviet Union in these circumstances. I must ask the house whether Canada's real interest would be promoted by a United States defeat. I must ask the house what such a defeat would mean by way of encouragement to an aggressive brand of political action. It is because of these considerations for Canada and other countries that we cannot deny the importance of this conflict in Viet Nam to us all.
I was impressed by the summary that the minister gave up to that point. Looking back at his report to the committee on external affairs last June, I found that he then took a serious view. If I may I will read a short quotation from pages 32 and 33 of the committee report. He was asked by the hon. member for York Centre:
What do you consider would be the consequences of an American withdrawal at this time?
The document reads:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think no doubt that there would be a complete overrun of the whole of Viet Nam by the north, and by the Viet Cong. The consequences of what the position China would be, I do not know. But the most serious part of all would be the consequences for Thailand, Burma, India, New Zealand, Australia, Malaysia, and the Philippines. What it would mean for us would be that the barriers would be brought closer to home, perhaps right to our own doorstep. While we must recognize that Asia must be allowed to work out its own destiny, and that it has great prerogatives, and that these must not be usurped by the west, nevertheless there is involved in this tragic situation the deepest implications for us, and for many countries with whom we have the closest ties.
That shows how serious the situation is in the mind of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I presume that he is express-

Supply-External Affairs ing the feeling of the government in that regard.
Attached as an appendix to the report of the minutes of the proceedings of that committee is a statement by the Minister of External Affairs for Australia, Hon. Paul Hasluck, given on the 23rd of March 1965. Australia is involved actively in the conflict in Southeast Asia. The Australian foreign minister said, and I quote from page 102 of the report:
In the circumstances that now exist, the United States could not withdraw from South Viet Nam without abandoning the responsibilities that belong to power or the principles they are trying to uphold. The United States could not withdraw without necessarily considering the world wide impact of such a withdrawal on the broader strategies of world politics.
If the United States did withdraw, the same conflict would be renewed somewhere else. Within a brief period the struggle now taking place in South Viet Nam would be shifted to Thailand. If there was abandonment of Thailand, it would shift to Malaysia-to Indonesia, to Burma, to India and further. Nothing would be ended and no stability would be achieved by yielding in South Viet Nam.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
There are other quotations I could give from the very able address by the Australian foreign minister. He viewed the matter with the greatest seriousness. And Australia is participating in the action in South Viet Nam.
What is Canada's policy? What did the minister say to us on January 25? He said that after he had drawn our attention to the seriousness of the situation he would turn to consider the policy he thought it right for Canada to follow in relation to that conflict. He dealt with our membership on the international commission. He stated there would be no sending of Canadian troops to Viet Nam. His words were as follows:
The government has no intention to recommend at any time the commitment of our forces to Asia unless pursuant to an obligation under the charter of the United Nations.
He went on to say:
Our policy has been intended to help bring the present conflict from the battlefield to the negotiating table.
I think those are the three main points of the policy he enunciated on that occasion. I put this question. If we accept the statement of the minister, supported by that of the Australian minister, that there would be the gravest consequences to the peace of the world if the United States were to withdraw from South Viet Nam and that our whole future would be affected by such a withdrawal, what is Canada's position with regard to this conflict?

Is it sufficient for us to hide behind our membership on the international commission?
The international commission was set up about 11 years ago. It operated in both North and South Viet Nam. At one time it had mobile teams which went about the country to see what was happening. I gather that for the past year the commission has been immobile. The teams were withdrawn from North Viet Nam and I doubt very much that anyone can move about either in the north or in the south without being in danger. So the international commission has not much scope for activity. The minister relied on a report of the commission in 1962.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As did the previous administration.
I beg your pardon?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As did the former government.

It showed that forces were being infiltrated to support those who were in rebellion in South Viet Nam. Then the minister drew attention to a report of February, 1965, when some contact was apparently made by the international commission with the government of North Viet Nam. But that is about all the commission has done in a period of almost four years. I wonder whether it can serve any useful purpose in the future. The minister says it gives us representation in Viet Nam and keeps the door open in case the situation can be brought to the negotiation table. But I do not hold out much hope of that while there are other forces at work and countries more powerful than Canada engaged in attempting to solve this problem.
The minister shelters behind our membership on the international commission. The Minister of National Defence, answering a question I put to him the other day, shielded himself behind the international commission.
I asked him whether the government was considering sending military observers to South Viet Nam to see what methods of warfare were being used in that area. I was not referring, as one correspondent suggested in a letter to me, to discovering how to kill women and children or to torture prisoners. That is nonsense. But if our armed forces are to reach peak efficiency as fighting forces they must be informed as to modern methods


of warfare, and the use of helicopters in South Viet Nam by the United States forces is something which should be studied by Canada. Military observers should be studying the methods used in waging jungle warfare and fighting against guerrillas. I do not think Canadian forces are trained sufficiently to take part in warfare of this type though some time in the future in some part of the world we may be compelled to engage in guerrilla fighting or jungle warfare.
I think we should not be sheltering behind our membership on the international commission. The minister makes a great point of bringing matters to the negotiating table. Everybody would like that to happen. No one is under any obligation in this day and age to say he is against war or that he is shocked by the horrors of war. I have heard for 50 years about the horrors of war. We do not need to beat our breasts and say "It is terrible". It is terrible. We have been afflicted in the twentieth century by warfare, and we still are. I do not know anyone who advocates war in order to kill people off. But we are faced with the necessity of looking at the realities of the situation. We are not free from the threat of war. We hope the balance of terror will save us from atomic and thermonuclear warfare but we are not safe from the perils of war by so-called conventional methods such as are now being used in South Viet Nam.
I see, Mr. Chairman, that private members' hour has come upon us. I will continue my remarks later.

That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all reports, briefs or other documents or communications received by the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General or the Department of Justice from the Law Society of Upper Canada relating to Mr. Justice Leo Landreville; all replies made to any such reports, briefs or other documents or communications; all letters or other communications addressed by the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General or any officer of the Department of Justice, since the first day of January 1964 to Mr. Justice Leo Landreville; all replies made by Mr. Justice Leo Landreville or by any solicitor or agent on his behalf, to any such letters or other communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when this motion was called yesterday the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) opposed it on grounds which I submit are both specious and evasive. I will deal succinctly with those grounds that he mentioned at that time because I do not intend to debate the matter at any length. I seek to have this motion come to a vote and let the free will of this house decide.
The independence of our judiciary is one of the most precious aspects of our constitutional heritage and this motion, Mr. Speaker, is designed not to violate it but to uphold it. That is its precise purpose. No member of this chamber has greater respect for the judiciary of this country than I. In this
Motions for Papers
chamber, and in the courts and elsewhere I shall always seek with all the diligence at my command to uphold the independence of the judiciary, its integrity and freedom from political interference. But I do not concede that the judiciary is above and beyond this high court of parliament.
It is not the conduct of Mr. Justice Landreville with which this motion deals. Let me make that abundantly clear. That will now be reported on by a commissioner, albeit I believe that royal commission to be a forum substituted improperly for this high court of parliament. What I am interested in is the conduct of the Minister of Justice and of his predecessor, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Favreau), the men responsible to this house, and I am not ready to let them hide behind any judicial cloak, any cloak of a royal commissioner or any phony argument about attacking the independence of the judiciary.
There is no doubt the Minister of Justice or his predecessor received a document from the Law Society of Upper Canada commenting upon the fitness for judicial office of Mr. Justice Landreville. Some members of this chamber have seen that document. There is no doubt a reply was sent to that document. The minister has stated this publicly on many occasions and he has consistently expressed willingness that the Law Society of Upper Canada should release the document.
Now the minister asserts that because I seek to have this document tabled in this high court of parliament I would be interfering with the independence of the judiciary or prejudicing a fair hearing for Mr. Justice Landreville. He has had no complaint about the governing body of the legal profession making the document public, but when a representative of the people seeks to end the mystery, the cloak and dagger atmosphere built up around this document-oh, well, that is very different. Oh, consistency, thou art a jewel.
The Minister of Justice has publicly stated that he asked Mr. Justice Landreville to resign. Did that public announcement from the Minister of Justice prejudice the independence of the judiciary? Did it prejudice a fair hearing for Mr. Justice Landreville? Oh, no, it is perfectly all right for the senior law officer of the crown to announce to the world that he had taken such a dim view of Mr. Justice Landreville's conduct that he had asked him to resign, but if a representative of

the people of Canada seeks to draw back the curtain of mystery and intrigue in the conduct of the Minister of Justice himself, that is very different. Poor Mr. Justice Landreville will suffer. What crocodile tears the minister weeps on his behalf.
How dreadfully his Lordship will be prejudiced before Mr. Rand, a jurist of the very highest repute, if this motion carries. What arrant nonsense do we hear from the lips of the very man who himself gaily announced to the world that poor Mr. Justice Landreville had been asked by him to resign.
No, Mr. Speaker, I repeat that his motion is not designed in any way to relate to the hearing now abdicated by this parliament to a retired judge. It is designed to get to immediate grips with the incompetence and inconsistency with which the Minister of Justice and his predecessor, the President of the Privy Council, have handled a vital matter affecting so delicately the whole principle of the independence of the judiciary in such a shoddy way. I say that in all ways the present Minister of Justice seems to have modelled himself on the President of the Privy Council, and he can be sure of the result that will attend upon that.
I want to point out that even in respect of this motion the Minister of Justice could not refrain from playing politics. The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) had a notice of motion on the order paper dealing with this subject and covering the first part of my motion. It was listed as No. 21 and therefore was on the order paper preceding mine, which is No. 39. But yesterday there was arranged the standing of the motion of the hon. member for York-Humber who is a supporter, though sometimes a maverick supporter, of the minister's party, in order to deal with this later motion by an opposition member. Is there anybody anywhere in this chamber who has any doubt of the reasons for this?
I have no doubt the minister will again seek to argue that the conduct of a judge may not be called in question under our rules except upon a substantive motion. There is no doubt about that being the case. It is stated in Beauchesne in citations 149(j) and 152(4). But as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out yesterday, I am not calling into question the conduct of any judge.
It is the minister and the government with whom I am concerned. When Mr. Rand

has reported there will be an opportunity again to concern ourselves in this highest court of the land with Mr. Justice Landreville.
Whatever I may think of the technique of the Minister of Justice in appointing a royal commission, I am now as anxious as any member of this house to ensure that Mr. Justice Landreville receives a fair and impartial hearing. No matter what happened, it could not be otherwise before a jurist so distinguished as Ivan C. Rand. But I am determined to hold the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres, who is now Minister of Justice, accountable for his conduct of the whole affair. For that reason I am asking hon. members in all parts of the house to support this motion, to strike a blow against the arrogance-I use that word deliberately- of the Minister of Justice, and his specious attempts to deprive this house of information to which it is genuinely entitled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the members of the Official Opposition feel that by speaking loudly and fast they can in this way convince the rest of the house to support their very poor arguments. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) speaks in very eloquent words of how he respects the independence of the judiciary. But no matter what he may say, the conclusion which he seeks, of having tabled in this house a report that concerns the activities of Mr. Justice Landreville, is in fact engaging in an exercise which does not respect the independence of the judiciary.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
One of the things I wanted to avoid in this case was the sounding of any political note; yet the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) managed in the short time he spoke to introduce this political note by claiming that arrangements had been made to eliminate motion No. 21 in order that the other hon. member's motion could be considered. In any event, one way or the other, the answer would be the same. As a matter of fact the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell), who is also the deputy leader of the house, had confirmed with the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) that he would not be here. It is for that reason the hon. member's motion came up. Is that a crime or something which, in respect of an important issue such as this, the hon. member should have mentioned?
It is all very well for the hon. member to speak of the arrogance of the government and the attitude of the Minister of Justice in
February 3. 1966

respect of a matter such as this, but does the hon. member realize that this is the first time since confederation the activities of a high court judge have been put into question? The procedures we are to apply now are extremely important. I would not, as Minister of Justice, want to introduce into this house a precedent which is contrary to what we have always believed in, the independence of the judiciary.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We are breaking new ground and we have had to go to British parliamentarians to discover procedure and to find out how to deal with this question. We should not, and this has not been the practice, discuss in any way the activities of a judge of the high court unless there is a substantive motion before the house which contains allegations of wrongdoing. I would not, as Minister of Justice, want to make allegations against Judge Landreville or any other judge until I was absolutely sure that something improper had in fact been done.
Why did the minister ask him to resign?
Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will go into that later. Mr. Speaker, the logical purpose of having an inquiry into this particular case is to enable us to have an independent inquiry made and to allow a consideration of all the aspects of the question, including the report of the Law Society and the negotiations that were involved.
I suggest it would be improper for us, Mr. Speaker, to bring this issue before this house before that inquiry was completed and unless the commissioner's report contained allegations of impropriety. At that time, and only at that time, could it be proper for a government and its minister of justice to come before this house with specific allegations of impropriety and a request for the establishment of a parliamentary committee composed of both houses, to be followed perhaps by a recommendation to the Governor General. That is the way, the fair way and the only way of handling this situation.
The hon. member has asked why I asked Judge Landreville for his resignation. I spoke with Mr. Justice Landreville some time last autumn and I asked him whether he did not think that in the circumstances it would be
Motions for Papers
advisable for him to resign. In reply he said: "Why should I? I have done nothing wrong." I did not pursue this any further.
Except to make it public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I made the statement public then and I am making it public now. I am not hiding the facts and why should I? What I am trying to do is make sure that the Law Society's report is considered on its face value and that Judge Landreville has an opportunity of having his say in court.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind hon. members that Judge Landreville did not have an opportunity of appearing before the Law Society in order to make his position clear.
Just like Mr. Spencer.
It is exactly the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Let us take these cases one at a time. There seems to be on the part of members opposite, particularly those who shout the loudest, some hypocrisy in this matter. What has been the attempt of this government? We have attempted to see that Mr. Justice Landreville has a fair hearing. We do not feel that we should in this house question the activities of Mr. Justice Landreville until we have received a report from the commissioner, Mr. Justice Rand.
I cannot see any reason, Mr. Speaker, why any member opposite should object to the procedure we have followed. I cannot see why they feel we are trying to hide something. We are not trying to hide anything. The government has nothing to hide in respect of this matter, nor does the government have to jeopardize uselessly the reputation of individuals to maintain its political image. In spite of the very eloquent plea made by the hon. member for Carleton, he has not convinced me that this report should be tabled. I believe we should wait until we receive a report from Mr. Justice Rand and then decide what this parliament should do in respect of Mr. Justice Landreville.

Mr. Speaker, what we in this house are worried about is, of course, the pattern that is emerging from the actions of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin). If we could believe that an employee in Vancouver, Mr. Spencer, would get the same type of treatment that is being afforded Mr. Justice Landreville, we might not feel quite so much like crying hypocrisy on this side.

speechtext: Order, please. I shall have to interrupt the debate at this point. I do not think there is any necessity at the moment for me to remind members of the very narrow limit of this debate. The issue before the house is whether or not certain documents should be tabled. While I recognize there must be some arguments dealing with the case before us, I feel that any argument in respect of any other case is quite out of order on the motion now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, with the greatest respect, what I was trying to do was draw a conclusion from a disquietening pattern that a good many of us feel is being exhibited by the present Minister of Justice for Canada, the person who should be the real guardian of the rights of citizens and who should protect those rights with as much vigour as he has displayed in his attempt to protect the judiciary. In any event I defer to your ruling, Mr. Speaker.
While we are speaking of unfairness, what does the minister really say about his conduct in publicly announcing that he asked the judge to resign? I think we are entitled to some consistency on the part of the minister and I think we are entitled to view his conduct with some disquiet.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
If the minister is not on television announcing the surveillance of a citizen, he is rushing to the newspapers to announce that he has asked a judge to resign. This is the pattern that disturbs us, a pattern emanating from the one man who should remove himself completely from this type of sordid conduct. The minister speaks of secrecy. I should like to remind him that on an earlier occasion in a debate about secrecy I had occasion to draw the attention of the house to a small book called "British Government Observed". The minister said he had to go to British precedents to find out how to deal with this judge. Perhaps he would like to go to a British professor of political science, who has written this small book, to find out about secrecy. I am going to remind the house of the conclusions of Professor Chapman:
It is only half the remedy to instil a more selfconscious feeling of public service into senior civil servants, and a more responsible attitude into

ministers. Both civil servants and ministers are inhibited by the habitual secrecy in which they are accustomed to carry out their operations, and which they must realize is at variance with any interpretation of public service. Honest and energetic men in government have an interest in opening up government, but they are required by the system to claim that it is impossible.
Just as the minister does today; he rushes to take refuge behind a rule.
They are therefore condemned to inaction, inefficiency, and permanent frustration.
This frustration, of course, is found in this house because of the minister's cloaking of his actions behind this rule.
This passion for secrecy has some constitutional support, but it clearly has much profounder psychological and sociological origins. Secrecy in public life panders to a craving for a sentiment of selfimportance, of belonging to an inner circle.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to say very much on the motion before the house except that I agree with the position taken by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) that this type of correspondence should not be made public at this time.
Like many at the bar, I have grave doubts about the wisdom of the Law Society in Toronto ever getting into this matter in the first place and purporting to pass judgment on a member of the judiciary. There is considerable doubt that this was the wisest course the society could have taken and there may be occasions in the future when they will have cause to regret it.
It seems to me-I am not purporting to speak for my party but only for myself- that the publication of documents of this kind at this time, particularly since this matter concerns a member of the judiciary, would probably create an even greater political climate around the whole question and would certainly greatly prejudice the work of the judicial inquiry under former Mr. Justice Rand, for whom all of us have a great deal of respect.
Speaking for myself, Mr. Speaker, as a member of the bar I am quite happy to wait until Mr. Justice Rand makes his report. I would not want to see anything done in the meantime that would in any way make more difficult the already very difficult and tenuous task that he has undertaken. I also think the minister has adopted the correct procedure in another regard. There was a discussion at one time whether this question should go before a committee of the House of Commons. I cannot think of anything that would have been worse, in my judgment, than to have referred this matter to a committee of the house. The
February 3, 1966

committee could not have helped devolving into a partisan wrangle, and notwithstanding some of our earlier qualms I think the minister is right in the course of action he has taken.
We are all very reluctant to deal with the whole problem of the judiciary and I think at this point the best course of action we could follow is the one the minister has followed, namely, appointing a highly respectable person to inquire into this question and leaving the whole matter and the correspondence involved out of the public purview until the commissioner has had a chance to report.

I am also a member of the bar of Ontario and I am as concerned as any other member of the bar or any other citizen of Canada about the independence of the judiciary. I should like to suggest to the minister, the members of the government, my learned colleague and all other members of this house, that there is another issue involved which seems to me to be at least as important as the issue of the independence of the judiciary. I refer to the way in which a citizen of a democracy looks upon the manner in which justice is administered in a democracy.
The administration of justice in a democracy depends, as almost everything else depends, on the consent of the people. The consent of the people depends on a conviction that every person in society is treated equally by the law and under the law. This seems to

me a much more important consideration than some other considerations which have been placed before this house.

Yes.

From the society.

I am not

saying that the minister is trying to do this. What I am saying is that the people who all of us here represent, our constituents, are saying in their minds that here is a judge, a lawyer, getting special treatment from the Minister of Justice. Mr. Speaker, I think
that question is best directed to the Minister of Justice. If the action of the Minister of Justice was wrong, I never did believe that two wrongs made a right, and I would remind the hon. member for Royal, who is a former attorney general, that perhaps he should be more aware of this fact than I.
This point emphasizes the more the argument I am making, that Mr. Justice Landreville did appear in court and was found innocent. On the surface he had the courage of his convictions to remain in his post as a judge. I would imagine the easy way out for Mr. Justice Landreville, whom we must presume innocent-I keep coming back to that point-would have been to retire from the bench and thus withdraw from the pangs and pressures of public opinion.

However, assuming that he is innocent, and I am convinced that the members of the House of Commons think that this man is innocent until proven guilty, how do we cope with the prejudice, intolerance and misguidance with respect to this matter that exists outside the House of Commons? The moral aspects of the case involving Mr. Justice Landreville are now to be examined by a royal commission. I am happy to say that nobody in the house during this hour or earlier has criticized the Minister of Justice on his choice of the man who will head the royal commission.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, there is another problem that is fairly fundamental to us, if I can just get away from the subject of Mr. Justice Landreville for the moment. I refer to the policy of production of papers in the House of Commons. This bothers me more than a little, because the question
February 3, 1966

comes up fairly frequently and many members are inclined to do their homework and to demand papers from the government.
From the little research that I have done on the subject, and I think this applies to the matter before us this evening, it has been indicated to me that the procedures, traditions and customs of the House of Commons of Canada are basically derived from those of the parliament of England. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) quoted an excellent authority tonight showing the degree of cynicism that exists in England and the preoccupation of the civil service and members of the government, comprising what is commonly referred to in England as the establishment or the inner circle, in preventing by all means possible the tabling of documents in general.
I found to my interest and perhaps to my dismay that the Official Secrets Act in England is so strange, so rigid and so all-embracing that it not only includes ex-ministers and ex-soldiers but even includes ex-contractors who have had anything to do with the government. The policy in England seems to be that under no circumstances do they give out documents if it is at all possible to prevent it.
Perhaps the time may have come for our own house to investigate the traditional method and to investigate the reluctance of the government at times to table documents. I think that here in Canada, as in England, we are adopting the viewpoint that all documents are private unless otherwise considered public. I think, Mr. Speaker, that once again we could learn a lesson with regard to the tabling of documents which would perhaps apply here, particularly if the case of Mr. Justice Landreville were not before a royal commission, which I think weakens the argument of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr Bell). In Sweden, Mr. Speaker, documents are considered to be public unless otherwise decreed secret. I think that the philosophy of the House of Commons of Canada should be a little closer to the philosophy of the Swedish system than that of England. I am sure you know that daily in the capital of Sweden, in large rooms placed at the disposal of the press, citizens, labour leaders and anyone else who is interested, there are placed all documents with the exception of those considered secret by the state.
I have noted the very enlightened, broadminded and objective attitude of the Swedish government toward the tabling of all docu-
Supply-External Affairs ments except certain categories which are considered and decreed to be basically and essentially secret in nature. Last year the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather), I believe, brought forward a particular bill which if it had been adopted would I think, have been very pertinent to the debate tonight. The bill was an act to better assure the public's right to freedom of access to public documents and to information about government administration. Its short title was, "Administrative Disclosure". Obviously, although the bill is rather abbreviated, the hon. member had based it upon the better features of the Swedish system. In that bill, Bill No. C-39, section 2 lays out four different categories which the hon. member would consider, if the bill had been adopted, as referring to documents that are confidential in nature and therefore it would not be in the best interests of individuals or society in general to divulge them with the same degree of freedom that is characteristic of documents outside these four points under the Swedish system.
One of them, Mr. Speaker, concerns documents affecting national security, a subject regarding which it is logical that disclosure of documents should be barred by statute. Then there are matters concerning subjects of private interest to the degree that the right of personal privacy excludes the public interest. The fourth provision had to do with trade secrets and commercial or financial information of a privileged or confidential nature obtained from private citizens.
Therefore I would humbly say to you, Mr. Speaker, that under the British system we should hardly be debating tonight the advisability of making documents public that could be relatively and increasingly important before the royal commission that will investigate the actions of Mr. Justice Landreville. May I say in conclusion, that even the very flexible attitude of the Swedish government would also exclude the request of the hon. member for Carleton because it does invade the private interests of Mr. Justice Landreville.

Mr. Chairman, before the break for private members' hour I was dealing with South Viet Nam and with Canadian policy in that connection. I was suggesting that if the government really relies on its assessment of the situation in South Viet Nam-I quoted something said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the effect that the situation is so serious that withdrawal of the United States forces might imperil the peace of the world-then it is important for us to consider what Canada is doing under the circumstances. I would suggest that to be shielded behind our membership on the international commission is not a satisfactory answer to account for our apparent inactivity. Then I was starting to deal with the question of bringing matters to the negotiating table, with which everybody agrees. If the situation can be negotiated and a peace settlement arrived at, that is fine. That was what was done in 1954 when France had spent about 10 years fighting in Indochina. How do you get the parties to the negotiating table? What is Canada's part in that enterprise?
[DOT] (7:00 p.m.)
I do not detract one bit from the activity of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his attempts to bring the parties together, and his constant suggestions that negotiation is the answer to this problem. But I think he is not dealing from strength and I am totally unimpressed by these constantly reiterated statements which tell us how bad war is and

how necessary it is that peace should be brought about through negotiation. Anybody can go around the world saying that. I was totally unimpressed by the activities of the Prime Minister when he visited the United States last spring and proposed a pause in the bombing of targets in North Viet Nam. speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit me to interrupt? I assure him that this was not the case.

I will take the minister's word for it. I said it looked to me as though it had been done in that way. Information seeps down. I think it was a faux pas in our international relations for the Prime Minister of this country to have gone down to the United States and suggested a course of action to the United States when they are so heavily involved in the war in South Viet Nam.
I reserve the right to criticize the United States on any occasion that seems fit to me. I have not always approved of what the United States has done. In both the first and the second world wars I thought the United States was somewhat reluctant to shoulder its burden. But ever since Pearl Harbour in 1941 the people of the United States have played their part in the world struggle and it is to them that we are looking for our own safety. And it ill-behooves us to criticize the activities of the United States in their present difficulties in South Viet Nam.
Hear, hear.

They may be wrong. Who knows? But they are committed and we are not. They are expending blood and treasure in order to prevent the spread of Communism in Southeast Asia. The minister has pointed out the danger to the world should the United States withdraw from South Viet Nam and should those other countries fall into the grip of Russia and China. It is not our job to criticize the best allies we have in the world. We talk about our peace keeping operations. We look with pride on what we are doing- and we are doing very well. There has been general agreement in Canada that we should undertake such operations as we have undertaken in the Congo, in the Gaza strip and in Cyprus. Well and good.

The United States and Great Britain have been conducting peace keeping operations ever since the end of the second world war. They have troops deployed all round the world. The United States has spent vast sums in ensuring that our defences against atomic attack are adequate or that our retaliatory effort will be adequate in the circumstances. That is peacekeeping, if hon. members are going to talk about peacekeeping. But for us to be criticizing what an ally is doing in Southeast Asia when we are doing nothing at all seems to me to be wrong. If I were an American I would say to Canadian representations: Put up or shut up. That is the way I would think about it.
My feelings would be as they were in the first world war when President Wilson was saying the United States was too proud to fight, and was writing notes to Germany. We who were over in Europe facing the Germans had nothing but scorn for that attitude. We had the same reluctance about approving the United States attitude from 1939 to 1941; and when the Commonwealth stood alone for an entire year the United States was on the sidelines, just as we are on the sidelines now with regard to South Viet Nam. I think it is wrong for us to get so exercised about what that nation is doing, and give advice to them.
We are terribly exercised about the bombing that is being renewed. I suggest to the minister that if the bombing is restricted to strategic targets, military targets, it is no different from artillery shells being directed against military targets. From my own experience I would rather take my chance with bombs from airplanes than with mortar fire, because airplanes often misdirect their bombs. If the bombing results in the death of women and children, of course that is shocking and bad. But if it is directed at military targets, what is the difference between aircraft bombing and artillery? I suggest to the minister we are not in a position of strength to give advice as to what should be done with regard to negotiation.
In the few minutes left to me I cannot elaborate fully, but I will refer to at least two things we could examine-whether we should take action or not, I do not know. The minister says we will not send troops to Viet Nam unless under United Nations authority. Well, the United Nations is unlikely to be involved in Viet Nam. There are procedures to be followed-technical matters-which prevent it. But why could we not provide medical and hospital services to the troops who

I am quite sure every member of parliament has had letters, as I have had, from people who protest Canada's expenditures on external aid on the grounds that we have a great deal to do at home and that we should be looking after our own people. Are we trying to hoodwink these people into believing that we are friends, with a voice on their behalf, or on behalf of the others? The greatest present imperialist nation is trying to hoodwink the nations of the world, and is trying to gain strength in its role of world history.
Now this, Mr. Chairman, I feel is tantamount to political hypocrisy. We should tell the truth. This was not so in the past. May I draw your attention to the fact that we are proud that Canada was one of the first nations to challenge Russian imperialism in the United Nations. In a speech in September of 1960, the present right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) declared that there must be a complete and final elimination of colonial regimes. He mentioned the
Supply-External Affairs fact that France and Britain and other powers have freed so many peoples. He threw the challenge to the Soviet Union, in these words:
How many human beings have been liberated by the U.S.S.R.?... How are we to reconcile the tragedy of the Hungarian uprising in 1956?... What of Lithuania, Estonia, Latvia? What of the freedom loving Ukrainians and many other eastern European peoples?
And he very emphatically stated:
There can be no double standard in international affairs.
Canada's voice was the first to be heard speaking emphatically and outspokenly in 1960.
The right hon. gentleman, now the Leader of the Opposition, was speaking to ethnic groups in Toronto in 1961, and he said:
The Soviet Union, while pretending otherwise, is a colonial power and a colossus of empires.
It dominates, subjugates, and exploits vast areas of Asia and of the Caucasus, initially colonized in the nineteenth century and earlier by Imperial Russia, using them as a source of cheap raw materials, cheap labour, and as a captive market.
He further stated, and I quote:
Soviet representatives will tell us that the peoples of these subject countries invited the Soviet army to invade them because what they wanted most was to become part of the Soviet Union.
No free country in the world invites or encourages invasion, or wants to be subjugated by another power. The right hon. gentleman further said this:
Is the Soviet Union to be the only colonial power remaining in the world? Why should the Soviet empire be more sacrosanct than any other? Different rules do not and should not apply to Soviet imperialists. There must be no double standards in the United Nations.
I might go on further. 1 quote from the records of the United Nations from the speech of the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) of November 23, 1962:
But what about the position of subject peoples within the Soviet empire? Assessments may vary but there are about 96 million people under Soviet rule who have never been permitted to exercise the right of self-determination which the U.S.S.R. so loudly proclaims for others. It is a unique and disturbing phenomenon at this time in world affairs, when one of the highest aspirations of mankind is the peaceful and orderly evolution to viable freedom for all dependent peoples, that the U.S.S.R. should continue to deny the rights of free election and expression to subject nations under its domination-
Mr. Chairman, that voice was not the only voice at the United Nations. May I quote here several sentences uttered by the late president of the United States. John Kennedy said

But that is why there is no ignoring the fact that the tide of self-determination has not yet reached the Communist empire, where a population far larger than that officially termed "dependent" lives under governments installed by foreign troops instead of free institutions.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Yet we in Canada are so happy to see these cultural exchanges with this so-called free nation, where everything is muzzled and where every nation associated with the so-called U.S.S.R., supposed to be a union, is exploited. We are silent. Is it because we are weak or because of other reasons? The President of the United States was not afraid to make the statement he did. The late Mr. Adlai Stevenson spoke the following words at the United Nations: "The right of self-determination has never been accepted within its own dependent areas by the Soviet Union.''
I feel that the Canadian people, the ethnic groups which are making such an effort to continue the fight for the freedom of their homelands and who hear such masterful orations from each one of us at their rallies, are entitled to hear what Canadian policy is on this subject-if we do have a policy. If we do not have a policy we might as well say so.
I associate myself with the hon. member for Oxford. I think that in the course of his address he covered many areas of the world which the minister chose to forget. Apparently we have no policy in these areas or, if we have, the minister preferred not to say anything about them. I think we are entitled to hear the minister's views on all the subjects which were raised by my hon. friend before the first item of these estimates is passed.
I agree with the minister that this is a subject near to my heart. This is not the first time I have spoken on it. I believe that in his heart the hon. gentleman agrees with me. But being a statesman is one thing and being a man who believes in the freedom of men seems to be another. I hope he will make a statement on this subject to this Canadian parliament. Otherwise, I will ask him these questions again.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Would the hon. member not do me the honour of saying he has read the statement to which I made reference-the statement made by myself as Secretary of State for External Affairs in the General Assembly on September 24?
[Mr. Mandziuk.i
DEBATES	February 3, 1966

I do not have the statement with me. I knew the minister had made one.
I am trying to point out that we are pussyfooting in these matters which are of such vital concern to a large number of the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, one usually begins a speech of this kind with a congratulatory preface about the minister's address. We cannot do that on this occasion. However, we can, I believe, congratulate the hon. gentleman upon his still being there. When one thinks of the great changes which have taken place in the cabinet to which he belongs one is reminded of a comment made by a member of the British house in similar circumstances when he congratulated a minister for "keeping his head while all about him were losing theirs". That is really an achievement. We are happy to see the hon. gentleman in this place and I am looking forward to hearing him speak, as he usually does, so eloquently, so well and so laconically.
A debate on the subject of external affairs is usually interesting, and this one, I believe, has been particularly so. As usual, hon. members have expressed a good deal of idealism. There is a tradition of idealism in the typical Canadian discussion of international questions. May it always be so. Great international movements have been founded on such idealistic sentiments as we have heard today. But also-and this, too, has been reflected 

there is an increasing recognition that we do live in an imperfect world among imperfect institutions and that international relations constantly reflect those imperfections. So we have to do many routine things in an effort to translate our ideas and ideals into the tangible results to which we all aspire.
As we look over the history of international institutions I think we have become more realistic while not losing sight of our goals. I am not old enough to remember the birth of the league of nations. But it was called, then, the hope of the world and there was a great deal of idealism attached to it. After its tragic failure and collapse, the new organization, the United Nations, was founded in an atmosphere of greater realism. I think the recognition of great power status, although we are often distressed by its manifestations, was a practical and realistic acknowledgement of the underpinnings of Realpolitik in the international field.
I was proud of the address given by the hon. member for Oxford. I know his merit in this field. He gave to the minister the benefit
February 3. 1966	COMMONS
of his experience, his knowledge and his concern. I suggest to the minister that he take careful note of what my hon. friend had to say. We would be very unwise to become too flippant about means, even though we realize there is a general unanimity as to ends.
The hon. and gallant member for Winnipeg South Centre spoke with his usual forthrightness and I think he hit many nails firmly on their heads. He raised some questions which many Canadians are raising. I was delighted that the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace should have made his maiden speech in the field of international affairs. I congratulate him on that, and on his speech. My hon. friend from Sherbrooke made some interesting comments. With one of these I heartily agree; with another, I resolutely disagree. I think it would be a most useful and helpful step for Canada to appoint an ambassador to the Vatican. I say this as one from a proud background in a section of the reform movement, Presbyterianism, which was rugged in its reformist tendencies.

Don't forget I showed you the monument to the reformers.
