Supply-External Affairs states. So, I am pleased the present Prime Minister went to Lagos and gave the leadership he did.
I am happy that we are developing more missions in Africa; but I would suggest that we do more, that we increase our interest and advance our priority to that important continent. I was shocked to read the other day that a request from Nigeria for documents, statutes of the Canadian government, had been refused. This was a shabby performance on the part of a Commonwealth state toward a proper request from a sister Commonwealth state, a federal state grappling with some problems for which they wanted this very small but practical bit of help. I condemn whoever was responsible for that particular little slip-up.
We are all distressed about Nigeria. There are many things in Africa that make us unhappy, but I think nothing is gained by those people who go about saying, "These people are not ready for self-government. They should hold down for a while until they are ready." Some would never be ready if they waited for the assistance that should have been forthcoming long since from those who had the opportunity to give it. No matter how feeble may be their efforts, as compared with our standards in administration of government, there is no gainsaying what I heard one of the representatives say some years ago at the United Nations-and he was quoting John Stuart Mill-that good government is no substitute for self-government.
We are faced with a problem when these people are yearning for self-government. They are able to attain it, and they will. Therefore we must make our adjustment. We must be as helpful as we can and not despair, and not too frequently project our own standards into theirs.
I heard a great statesman a very few years ago-I know the minister knows him well, a former President of the United Nations General Assembly, Ambassador Boland-say that the future of the world will be decided by the people who live south of the equator. I believe that to be the case. The rapid developments that are taking place there are a bit overwhelming. They overwhelm our understanding, and perhaps at times they may challenge and overwhelm our capacity to assist.
This brings me to the question of Latin America and the O.A.S. I know the Secretary of State for External Affairs will expect me to say that I disagree on this matter with my

hon. friend from Oxford, and I know there are other members in my party who have views similar to his. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek and the hon. member for Yarmouth-Shelburne-Clare are both anti-
O.A.S., but I am with the minister, or at least with him as he used to be, as one of those who believe that there is an opportunity for us.
Just because there is difficulty, and just because there is the possibility of our differing with the United States, these things alone should not be sufficient cause for Canada to withdraw, forever to stay on the sidelines from an area of the world whose future will affect us whether we are members of that organization or not. Any eruption of major proportions in Latin America will not be magically sealed off at the 49th parallel just because we would not take out membership in the O.A.S. Therefore I would say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that if he and his government are interested in making a move along this line, here is at least one member of the opposition who would be prepared and willing to support them. They have been able to get by on tougher issues with only five of a majority. In this case there might be four others over here. Also, members of the N.D.P. who used to be pretty strong on this issue. Therefore I think it would not be a hazard and might even be an easy thing.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
We have been discussing the O.A.S. for a long time. I think we have been able to disagree with the United States and survive, and I think we are now sufficiently mature in the field of international diplomacy to move in and accept our responsibilities. If we wait until all these problems move away; if we refrain from joining because they make mistakes in their organization and because it is imperfect, we will never join and we might as well withdraw from all the other organizations of which we are members because there is a great deal of imperfection in all of them. I think the opportunities and challenges are sufficient to prompt us to want to join, and I am looking forward to the great opportunity of supporting my hon. friends on this matter. However, I do have the feeling that I will not have that opportunity soon to stand up, perhaps alone among my friends, to join with them. However, if they present the opportunity I will present myself as living testimony of faith in the movement toward the

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, during his very trenchant speech discussed Viet Nam, as other hon. members have done. I may say that I was surprised by the reply the Prime Minister made to my hon. friend, the leader of the New Democratic Party, on January 24 when he said:
I can also assure him that there is no possibility of military aid being sent by Canada to Viet Nam.
I do not look forward to Canadian military aid being sent. I do not relish the prospect of Canadian youth being there. I pray to God they never will have to be there, but I submit that the Prime Minister overstated the case when he spoke as he did. It is sadly conceivable that situations may arise where the interests of Canada and her people, and the foreign policy to which we are dedicated, may require tangible assistance on the spot. I think the Prime Minister overstated the case in ruling that out in advance. I would by all means commend to the government the course of action advocated by my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. We should be sure, knowing the possibilities of outbursts of this kind, that our armed forces are capable of playing their part if, heaven forbid, that becomes necessary.
Wishing that Viet Nam and all its problems would go away is just about as futile as imploring the United States to leave. Some people advocate that as a solution if only the Americans would withdraw all would be well they say. It is said about the United States, with its complexity and its vastness, that it is a diificult country to govern. If only their leaders could come to Canada and stay a while they would be told very simply how to do it. Big business in Canada tells its government how to conduct their economic policies; big socialism tells them how to conduct their diplomacy and, as if that were not enough, we now have provincial politicians telling them generally how to do everything. How simple it all is north of the 49th parallel.
I know that we all join with equal sincerity the utterances of hon. members and Canadians outside of this house who deplore the war in Viet Nam. What kind of people would we be if we did not have that kind of reaction in the face of intense suffering and loss of life. Of course we deplore it, yet we find it very difficult-at least I do-to join the chorus of those who would point to the United States as the culprit in this affair.
The United States has shown, especially in recent weeks, much restraint and wisdom. A while ago there was a pause, and that was
Supply-External Affairs supposed to solve all things. That pause lasted for nearly six weeks, but the response from the other side was not very encouraging. I think the United States is to be commended for bringing this whole situation to the United Nations. I know the purists talk about the fact that Geneva is the only avenue and that communist China could be there, but now we have the Viet Nam situation at the Security Council. We have had a pause and we have now had a statement from the United States, that leader of the free world, welcoming, seeking, beseeching and negotiating a settlement. I am never distressed, as some are, that Canada does not disagree more with the United States. Disagreement for the sake of disagreement would be a very immature concept of Canada's role.
I say to the hon. minister that in his general attitude toward the major aspects of world diplomacy and the leadership of the United States he speaks for the great majority of Canadians as represented in this house. He follows quite a tradition. I had the honour of seeing his two predecessors in action, Howard Green and the late Dr. Sidney Smith. They were men of stature, men of vision, tough men when they needed to be tough, and he is following generally in their steps. He is following not as quietly at times but, as Mr. Green once said, he is a good internationalist. I hope that in this area, where we do not want foreign policy to become party policy, he will heed carefully the advice of those who have spoken. I think he will agree that his government might have avoided many pitfalls in the last good many months had they heeded better what the opposition said.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
So I say to him that we wish him well. His task is not easy. He has made mistakes and they have been pointed out, but I believe our country still holds the good opinion of the world. Sometimes we are perhaps a bit selfrighteous about how good we are, but as a middle-sized, moderate country prepared to take its share we may well be proud of Canada in the discharge of its international obligations.
Mr. Chairman, because everybody is yearning to hear the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I am sure there are other hon. members who wish to contribute to this debate, I shall follow his example of today and be brief and sit down.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some hon. members may recall their days in high school when they had to figure out a Pythagorean theorem, where a man is trying to catch up with a turtle a few feet ahead of him. Logically, the man could never catch up with the turtle because every time he took a step forward the turtle was also stepping ahead a few inches, and therefore the two would never meet. However, some sort of intuition must have suggested to this logician that the meeting would occur in spite of the mind's objections.
It seems to me that the international situation to-day can be compared to that theorem. Since the end of World War II, countries have united to launch, this time, the peace offensive.
As in the theorem, however, these common agreements would or should have brought peace. Yet, since the end of World War II, in one corner of the earth or the other, not a day passes without war. Yet, an inner feeling tells us that the great objective of peace always remains a possibility.
I humbly feel that a link is missing, or rather a dimension without which world peace cannot be achieved. This dimension to my mind, is the entry of Communist China into the United Nations. It would be futile to recall the powerlessness of the United Nations Secretary General, of his Security Council on the Viet Nam question.
That is why, and it is the only aim of my intervention today, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) to use all his influence to secure the agreement of the United States to the admission of mainland China to the Council of Nations, the first step, I think, toward a solution to the Asian war.

Mr. Chairman, as will become more evident, we are not here as experts. However, as one who has been interested in the methods that this house adopts to get its point of view across to the public, I have been a critic-I must say not a very severe one-of a good many debates on this important topic because I think many times, I suppose because of the crush of business, we have really not had a debate but we have had a series of position papers, if you like that expression, from the representatives of the parties that make up parliament. So I welcome an opportunity to say one or two things that have been on my mind about this awesome topic.
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
I should like to do so by first of all reminding the committee that really we are part of a world that is in what might be classified as a three-way split. First is our world, representing as it does 700 million people, about 20 per cent of the total world population. Then there is the world that represents about 30 per cent of the world population that is under the domination, if you will-although this is perhaps an old-fashioned term-of Communism; anyway, it is part of the Communist ideology. I think that in any discussion of this part of the world we have come to learn that this term does not mean the same thing to different countries, and I welcome the fact that this has become now clearly part of the United States understanding of world affairs.
Then surely on our minds must be the third part of the world, that part that I know concerns the Secretary of State for External Affairs as it does all of us if we are responsible members of parliament. I refer to that immense area of this globe the peoples of which are still living in the most abject poverty, with a gross product representing only about 15 per cent of the world's productive wealth. Surely we should continue to think about this fact and remember the potential danger-it has been mentioned by other speakers-if this split, if that is the term, or this divergence should become escalated. I suggest that this is really the context in which the Secretary of State for External Affairs discharges his very awesome responsibilities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, to come from that soaring introduction to one or two practical things that are on my mind, I should like again to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the officers and staff of the Department of External Affairs across the world still have not the opportunity to vote in elections. Surely by this time a simple method could be worked out whereby these people could exercise their franchise. Surely it is a paradox that in so many of our embassies the military personnel attached thereto are able to vote, and yet our distinguished Canadians who are ambassadors, senior officials, attaches, charges d'affaires, and so on, cannot take part in this democratic process.
I have heard the excuse used that a good many of our people in other parts of the world do not know what is going on-perhaps I should not use that expression but should say they are not conversant with attributes of the various candidates. Surely in this age of
February 3. 1966

improved techniques of communication it should not be too difficult to rectify this situation. I am sure that each of us would be glad to cut down his budget at election time to make available information that our embassy people need to have before making up their minds with respect to choosing candidates. I hope that the minister will quickly set in motion amendments to the Elections Act so that this reform can take place.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
Then, there is a letter to which the minister recently subscribed his name replying to a request for funds for the Canadian Peace Research Institute in the modest amount of $35,000, by means of which the institute would set up a peace research abstract system. I understand that UNESCO gave this worthy group some $6,000. Surely, with our huge defence budget and our other budgets, the modest request of this most worth-while group could be met gracefully by the minister. I am sorry that he has not seen fit to do so.
We have heard a great deal, and quite properly, about Viet Nam. I am not going to add very much to the knowledge of the country about this tragic war, except to say that generally I agree with the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) when he says it is extremely easy for us in Canada to criticize. It does seem to me that the auspices for President Johnson's request for action by the Security Council would have had much more validity had he been able to continue the break in the bombing of North Viet Nam until he or his ambassador had made that presentation. I do not suppose it takes a very learned or expert person to think of this, but I say it for what it is worth.
One of the things that has worried me a little bit about our United States friends and their debate on this topic has been that, up until recently, it has been considered almost an act of treason-I use that word advisedly in quotes-if one took issue with the views of the President. This makes me think back to the days of the second world war when in Britain, even though Sir Winston Churchill headed a coalition government, he insisted that parliament continue to comment upon and criticize the government's prosecution of the war and its resultant foreign policy. I do not know how gracefully he insisted, but he did insist. I think it is a refreshing thing for the friends of the United States to see that distinguished senators are able to dissent. It
Supply-External Affairs was not too many months ago that the only dissent a good many of us were able to discern was the peace marches, estimable as they may be, and the editorials of the New York Times, as well as the remarks of that great pundit Walter Lippmann.
I think it is refreshing to note that the chairman of the United States Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and other senators, have been taking an independent position in what must be a terribly serious thing for our friends in the United States.
The people in this land have different ideas about Rhodesia. I share those expressions about our Prime Minister's trip to Lagos, and the worry about the advisability of our Prime Minister being in Lagos and being seen to the plane by the Prime Minister of that country, who was to be executed within hours of the Prime Minister's leaving. I suppose nothing really in recent history has been of more comfort to Mr. Ian Smith than the events in Nigeria. Some years ago, I had the privilege of visiting Rhodesia and meeting and admiring, as I am sure we all do, Mr. Garfield Todd.
I often think back to those days and wonder whether anybody who was in Africa five or ten years ago could ever have imagined that, for instance, Kenya would prove to be a model of the evolutionary process from colo-nialsim and that Rhodesia would be otherwise. I just add this for the record. One of those in Africa with me was Mr. Edward Heath, now the head of the Conservative party in Britain. I remember so clearly one man saying: If the governor would make me a colonel and let me raise an army, I would solve the Rhodesian problem. Mr. Heath quite quickly said, what colour shirts would your army wear?
I think that when we reflect on the views of our friends in the United States about world affairs we should commend Senator John Pastore's resolution in the United States senate, in which he seeks to curb the proliferation of nuclear arms. I think that these are the types of positive United States beliefs that we in Canada should support.
I just want to read to the house two of the prime purposes behind Senator Pastore's resolution. They are:
A provision requiring non-nuclear states to accept international safeguards over all nuclear activities; a provision also requiring nuclear states not to transfer nuclear material to other nations for civilian purposes except under international safeguards.

In addition this resolution hopes that steps will be taken to bring chemical reprocessing plants under international inspection.
I have one other thing I should like to mention, and I apologize for bringing in another personal reference. Last June it was my privilege to be in San Franscisco attending a small meeting preliminary to the twentieth anniversary meeting of the United Nations. This meeting was held under the auspices of a great United States citizen-I think he is anyway-Mr. Maxwell Stanley. He is active in the world federalists. With that generosity that is so typical of the people of the United States, he invited some 15 people from various countries of the world to take a look at the UN a decade hence.
People like Carlos P. Romulo, formerly the President of the General Assembly of the United Nations and past president of the Philippines, Sir Safrulla Khan, whose name will be known to the minister as a president of the assembly and also now in his second term in the world court of justice, attended. I will not bore the house by referring to each of the participants. After four or five days of deliberations in a pleasant atmosphere detached from the pressures of the day, several conclusions were reached. These were presented by Carlos P. Romulo at this meeting of world federalists. The text was a belief that we cannot wait for greater understanding and brotherhood to bring us these freedoms, but we must begin now.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Changes were suggested in the United Nations, one of which was referred to by the hon. member for Quebec South a minute ago.
I am sure these changes would have widespread approval in this house. The UN would have to be greatly strengthened to provide these essential requirements for peace.
The changes suggested were, first of all, complete and enforced disarmament of all nations, in carefully controlled stages. When the disarmament process is complete, each nation would retain only strictly limited and lightly armed forces for internal order. Significant progress in disarmament will not be possible without parallel progress toward the provision of international security through the United Nations.
The second requirement would be a permanent UN peace force to maintain international peace and security; and an effective


UN inspection system to supervise disarmament. Again that is an objective which I am sure would find favour with all of us.
The third requirement would be a general assembly empowered to adopt binding rules and regulations in respect to the peace keeping functions of the strengthened UN and implementing the disarmament plan; and in the opinion of most but not all of the conferees, a revised voting system appropriate to the strengthened UN, including abolition of the present "veto power" in the Security Council.
The proviso in this submission was that a good many countries are faced with the paradox of having equal representation, no matter what their population. This fact is well known to the minister and to most members here. For example, we face the situation that Iceland, say, with somewhat less than 100,000 people, and India with somewhat more than 400 million people, have equal voice in the United Nations. This is a situation that we politicans have had to look after in this country for our own benefit through the means of redistribution. Quite how this would work on a world scale I am not sure, but perhaps there would have to be a weighting of votes. No country would have less than one vote, but perhaps the great powers would agree that they have, say, 30 votes. This is a fact of life which must be faced in any event.
The fourth proposal was a strengthened court of justice empowered to interpret the UN charter and decide all international legal disputes; a system of regional courts; and other tribunals and agencies to settle international disputes which are not capable of decision upon legal principles. Membership in the United Nations should carry with it the acceptance of the jurisdiction of the international court in all international disputes.
The fifth requirement would be a world development program. As a matter of human survival, the world must use a substantially larger share of its resources to promote the economic and social advancement of the less developed nations. Expansion and better coordination of existing development programs are urgently needed. A major part of the savings from disarmament should be used for a large scale development program administered by the United Nations.
The sixth requirement would be a reliable and adequate revenue system for the strengthened UN. Surely one of the tragedies of current days is the hat-in-hand manner in which the United Nations has to circularize
February 3, 1966
the nations in order to carry on their peace keeping activities in Cyprus and in so many other parts of the world.
The seventh requirement would be safeguards to prevent abuse of power by the strengthened United Nations, and a clear reservation to the member states and their peoples of all powers not granted to the UN under the revised charter. Hon. members who are constitutional lawyers can imagine that the Canadian delegate to this meeting, as well as the Americans, wrestled with this one a little longer than did those from other nations of the world to whom the semantics of constitutionalism mean very little.
The last requirement would be eligibility of all nations for membership in the United Nations. Disarmament will not be possible unless all nations are subject to the enforcement system.
These are the unanimous recommendations of the conference I had the privilege of attending. It was a conference on the United Nations as we foresaw it in 1975. I would conclude by saying that I subscribe to these proposals. I am convinced that they have validity, and I hope that the minister, when he is thinking of what should be done to ensure peace, will keep them very much to the front of his mind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have had a wide-ranging and useful discussion. I feel that I owe it to the committee to deal with one matter put before us in respect to a current situation. It was introduced by the official spokesman for the Conservative opposition in this house. Because the matter is current I propose to address myself to it now. I will deal with other items as they come up during the course of my estimates.
I must say that in view of the widespread and almost overwhelming world support of the position taken by Her Majesty's government in the United Kingdom with regard to the illegal government in Rhodesia, I was a little surprised at the position adopted by the hon. member for Oxford. Whether he was speaking for his party is perhaps not clear. In any event, he was its first spokesman. Because of the importance of the question and the challenge which he laid down to the government both with regard to the authority under which it had acted and his implied criticism of the reasons for its policy, I owe it to the committee to make a reply.
His statement today was made in the context of a rather regrettable situation which
Supply-External Affairs has persisted now in Southern Rhodesia for over three or four years, during which time the parliament and the government of that country has adopted a number of acts providing for detention of political opponents of the regime, contrary to what we in Commonwealth countries regard as the rule of law.
Under these acts nationalist parties have been outlawed and a number of leading political figures, both African and European, have been detained or restricted as to residence without a trial or hearing. There has been an extended form of racial discrimination, not of the identical character of apartheid, but of a character which, in face of the present evolution of world opinion on the position of the human being in society, cannot be condoned.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
One form of racial discrimination is the franchise which, as a result of financial and other qualifications, enables the small minority of Europeans to have the predominant voice in the legislative body of Rhodesia. Other legislation reserves much of the best agricultural land in Rhodesia to the use of white settlers, providing a form a discrimination which, in light of what we regard as the current standards of enlightenment and acceptance of human personality, cannot be condoned, and is not condoned I think by the vast majority of the people in this country. Nor can it be condoned by the vast majority of the members of this house, or by the vast majority of the peoples of the commonwealth.
Since last November, or since the unilateral declaration of independence, the Smith regime has imposed a press and radio censorship which to a great extent insulates the people of Rhodesia from outside news and which enables the regime to give unchallenged its own version of events.
It is not as though the government of Canada had acted without careful consideration and anticipation of this decision. It will be noted from our records in this house that long before there was definite indication that there would be a unilateral declaration of independence, both the Prime Minister and I had indicated what our position would be in such an event.
At the prime ministers' conference in London, in June of last summer, the Commonwealth prime ministers without exception indicated their opposition to the threatened unilateral declaration of independence. I may say that well over two years ago I, myself,

February 3, 1966

Supply-External Affairs had received as Secretary of State for External Affairs two ministers of the then government of Southern Rhodesia in my office in the Department of External Affairs. I had explained to them our attitude toward events in that country, events which were discussed not only at Commonwealth meetings, but in the United Nations itself. May I say that as a result the government of Mr. Smith was not taken unawares by the action of the government of Canada.
While I have no right to speak for other governments in the Commonwealth, it is a fact that these governments likewise made their positions known, both at the conference of prime ministers, and bilaterally. I might add the record will show that the Prime Minister of Canada had urged in private communications, as I did, that the government of Rhodesia should take full consideration of the implications of the step which it took some time last November.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman in his implied criticism of this position by the Canadian government, questioned at the same time the authority under which we have acted, and sought to indicate that this represented a departure in Canadian foreign policy. I will admit, with him, that it represents an approach that has not been practised by Canadian governments until recently. Certainly, any action of a punitive kind within the commonwealth must be examined with the greatest care. Indeed that has been the situation in the particular instance. However, this is not the first time that we have acted in this way. It should be noted that in this instance we have acted pursuant to a resolution of the Security Council of the United Nations, just as we did in the case of South Africa. Our action then was based on a resolution passed by the Security Council in 1963.
Because the matter does represent, even though it may not be the first precedent, an important development in Canadian foreign policy, I think it might be worth while to remind the hon. gentleman of the action that Canada took toward South Africa pursuant to the resolution of the Security Council in 1963. The house will recall the statement I made on October 21, 1963 with respect to the export of arms from Canada to South Africa, to the effect that the Canadian government would not permit the shipment of arms to South Africa. We had not been permitting arms exports to be used against anyone for the enforcement of the policy of apartheid. In

1963 the Security Council passed a resolution that was not mandatory, but that did recommend that all states should cease the sale and shipment of arms, munitions and military vehicles to South Africa. We took that into account, and as a loyal member of the United Nations and wishing again to express our disapproval of the South African apartheid policy the government felt that it should not authorize the acceptance of any new orders from South Africa for items of military equipment, or permit the shipment of such equipment to South Africa. That was done not long after the action taken by the government of which my hon. friend was a supporter, which represented Canada during the prime ministers' conference, following which South Africa took action resulting in its withdrawal from the Commonwealth.
No. They withdrew before. That has no bearing on it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I respectfully say to my hon. friend that this has a great bearing, because my hon. friend has put himself in a position different from that of his leader.
Oh no, no.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: His leader expressed at that time some of the sentiments of the people of Canada. I want to be very clear on this, because it is important.
Then you will have to try harder.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: His leader at that time took a strong position. I am not saying that his leader's acts led to the withdrawal of South Africa from the Commonwealth, but he did join with other prime ministers in expressing what was then, in my judgment, the view of most people in this country and the Commonwealth. In this day and in this age the policies of discrimination as practised by South Africa cannot be condoned.
No one says that they should be.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My friend says no. I am saying that the action that he has taken in his utterances today with regard to Southern Rhodesia are inconsistent with the position taken by the right hon. gentleman, the Leader of the Opposition, when he was prime minister, with regard to South Africa.

Would the minister not think that there is a difference in that situation, inasmuch as at the time when South Africa
February 3, 1966

became a republic, and automatically left the Commonwealth, and had to seek to return, there was a question of whether South Africa should be admitted back into the Commonwealth in view of her policies. Would that not show that there was some difference in the position from the standpoint of Rhodesia's withdrawing from the Commonwealth?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
All I can say to
my hon. friend is that if we want to preserve the unity of the Commonwealth, and I believe that it is a vital organism for international collaboration, we cannot in any way give any comfort to those who, by implication or otherwise, seem to support a policy of racial discrimination.
With regard to the sanctions that the government did impose on South Africa, which was a precedent for the development of Canadian foreign policy, may I say that in 1964 there was a call by South Africa for tenders for certain military vehicles. In light of the announced Canadian policy, no Canadian company responded to the tenders called for these vehicles. This was a result of Canadian government policy based on a resolution of the Security Council. All trucks capable of being used for military purposes, came within the meaning of the resolution.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
This course Canada took, notwithstanding the fact that one or two commonwealth countries continued to allow corporations within their jurisdiction to tender for the sale of this equipment in South Africa in a way we felt and continue to feel was unfair to the Canadian position and to the clear interpretation of the Security Council resolution.
The government's policy with respect to military assistance to Portugal was announced in the house on June 25, 1963. This related to certain kinds of equipment. We have delivered no mutual aid to Portugal since November, 1960. Earlier shipments to Portugal as to other NATO countries had been made on the understanding that they would be used only to strengthen the defensive capacity of the organization. Likewise, we have stood in the way of sales of equipment to that country except for purposes involved in its obligations under the NATO agreement. So the situation taken with regard to Portugal is consistent with the position we have taken with regard to South Africa and the position we are now taking with regard to Rhodesia.
Supply-External Affairs
The hon. member today questioned the wisdom of the sanctions upon which the government has decided. Not only did he question this, but he doubted whether we had the authority to impose them. He indicated that parliament should have been called to express an opinion before they were imposed. I ask him to consider the circumstances in which these sanctions were applied. The parliament of the United Kingdom had been sitting and was sitting at the time. The British government did not hesitate to announce to the U.K. parliament that it had adopted a particular course based on acts which were in some respects similar to ours. It left to the parliament of the United Kingdom the opportunity to reject or approve the course the government had taken.
But our parliament was not sitting. We had to act quickly. We were amongst the very first countries to act. I can well envisage what the hon. member would have said had we waited unduly long before imposing sanctions when there had been a call for us to do so by the government of Britain.
Why was parliament not called?

In any event the measures were taken immediately after the illegal declaration of independence announced on November 11. They consisted of nonrecognition of a regime dismissed from office by the lawful authority, the governor of Rhodesia. A number of allied and appropriate actions were included in these measures. We withdrew our trade commissioner. We ended our small aid program, imposed a complete arms embargo and withdrew the British preferential tariff rate as well as export credit facilities for Canadian goods going to Rhodesia. These measures were essentially direct and natural consequences of our nonrecognition of an illegal regime which had been dismissed from office. They were taken in accordance with similar measures taken by the British government, which we recognized as being constitutionally responsible for Rhodesia.
The action we took was similar to that taken by the government of the United Kingdom by executive authority, acting within the legal powers of that government. Similarly the action taken by other countries such as Sweden, Australia, and New Zealand, countries in NATO and outside, was taken pursuant to the authority they had. If their

February 3, 1966

Supply-External Affairs parliaments were sitting, they had I presume an opportunity to deal with the matter.
We would have been accused by the hon. gentleman of undue delay had we failed to act as quickly as we did. The hon. member questions the legality of the ban on the export of arms. It is the policy of the government not to permit the shipment of arms and military equipment to troubled areas such as Rhodesia. Because of the illegal declaration of independence we felt the export of arms would be wrong. I may say by way of parenthesis that long before the unilateral declaration of independence was made by the government of the country concerned, it received an intimation of the course which would be followed by this and by other commonwealth countries. By order in council under section 3(A) of the Export and Import Permits Act our export control list has been in existence for some time now. The effect of this is to make the export of sensitive goods subject to permit for shipment to any destination. This was the legal authority for refusing to ship arms to Rhodesia. As to the withdrawal of export credit facilities, it is entirely within the discretion of the government under the Export Credits Insurance Act, as amended, to decide whether a particular country is eligible for financing under section 21 (A) of that act.
We now come to the second phase of Canadian measures following the Security Council resolution of November 20 which, as I mentioned earlier, recommended the severance of all trade ties with Rhodesia under the illegal regime. It was pursuant to this resolution that our subsequent economic measures were taken, namely the export and import bans and the withdrawal of insurance facilities for exports. This was in accordance with the established Canadian policy of acting on Security Council recommendations and, in general, of giving strong support for United Nations action in situations with serious international repercussions.
I want the hon. member to know that the action we took with regard to Rhodesia was, as in the case of South Africa, pursuant to recommendations made by the United Nations itself. The hon. member has said that these export and import bans were illegal.
Only some of them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member says some of them were. Shortly after the passage of the November 20 Security Council resolution and in keeping with our policy of acting in concert with Britain, with was

constitutionally and legally responsible for the territory of Rhodesia, we concluded an arrangement with the British government providing for close co-operation in the application of further economic measures against the illegal regime of Rhodesia. This arrangement took the form of an exchange of notes on November 26 between the Canadian and British governments-actually between myself and the British High Commissioner. As Secretary of State for External Affairs I asked that the Department of Justice be consulted. We were advised that an exchange of notes between Canada and Great Britain, the latter as the sovereign power in Rhodesia, providing for the application of economic sanctions against Rhodesia, was an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment within the terms of the Export and Import Permits Act.
So we have been advised by the law officers that the course we have followed was legal and warranted under the legislation. The hon. member will, I am sure, take note of what I have said tonight. And if he thinks that what I have said or what the law officers have put forward is wrong, he will no doubt give the house the benefit of his learned opinion.
Myself and others.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As for insurance of exports of goods or services to a particular country, the Export Credits Insurance Corporation has authority under the act to insure or not to insure at its discretion.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
My hon. friend referred today to the various orders in council and I want to assist his researches in that regard. PC 1965-2016 of November 12 provided for the withdrawal of preferences and the application of the general tariff to imports from Rhodesia pursuant to subsection 1 of section 4 of the Customs Tariff.
That is all right.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend said that one was all right. In one breath he says we acted illegally, and now he says in regard to that particular order we acted within the meaning of the law.

If the minister had looked at the remarks I made-he could have seen the blues-he would have found I said that two or three of the orders were perfectly legal. It was those under sections 5 and 6 of the
February 3/ 1966

Export and Import Permits Act that I questioned. I questioned the legality of them. That was the embargo on sugar, tobacco and chrome ore.
Do I understand he does not take exception to the legality of PC 1965-2134 respecting the imports of tobacco and sugar of Rhodesian origin?
I have done so.

PC 1965-2134 of November 30 provided for the addition to the "import control list" of tobacco and sugar of Rhodesian origin, pursuant to section 5 and 6 of the Export and Import Permits Act, and to implement an intergovernmental arrangement between Great Britain and Canada.
That was one. I questioned the legality of it, not the one under the Customs Tariff Act.

Well then, my hon. friend takes issue with the position we have taken and the advice we have been given. I think it is clear, reading the act, and assuming the existence of an intergovernmental arrangement such as the one I have tabled between the government of the United Kingdom and Canada, that it is self-evident we followed the proper legal procedure.
PC 1965-2211 of December 8 provided for the addition to the "import control list" of the following items of Rhodesian origin: chrome ores and concentrates; ferrochrome, asbestos and meats, pursuant to sections 5 and 6 of the Export and Import Permits Act; and likewise in conjunction with the intergovernmental arrangement between Britain and Canada, I submit we had the legal authority for this course.
Finally, PC 1965-2252 added Rhodesia to the area control list pursuant to sections 4 and 6 of the Export and Import Permits Act. I take it my hon. friend does not take exception to that.
Am I right in concluding that the minister is relying entirely upon the phrase "intergovernmental arrangement" for his authority?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Well, it is clear that the resolution of the Security Council was not mandatory. The only way in which we could act under the Export and Import Permits Act would have been with regard either to a mandatory obligation or in respect of an intergovernmental arrangement. We had an intergovernmental arrangement. My

Supply-External Affairs hon. friend has a copy of it in his hand. Our action was brought clearly within the Export and Import Permits Act. This was the advice of the officers of the crown.

May I ask a further question, because this is very interesting. The letter from the British High Commissioner, in the second paragraph, reads that he is authorized to confirm on behalf of the government of Great Britain and Northern Ireland that they think it desirable and important that they and the government of Canada should arrange to co-operate closely in this field. Do I take it that the minister considers the phrase "to co-operate closely in this field" is the "governmental arrangement" to impose sanctions?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend, I think, has stated the case admirably.
Finally, the reference to an intergovernmental arrangement in the paragraphs I have related, meant that the Export and Import Permits Act could be used, as the hon. gentleman has just said, in relation to an intergovernmental arrangement or commitment which was duly entered into between the government of Canada and the United Kingdom. Such an engagement was entered into between the two countries through an exchange of notes which have been tabled and which, in the opinion of the law officers of the crown, meets the exigencies provided for by the phrase "intergovernmental arrangement" referred to in the act.
So, as a result of the addition of Rhodesia to the area control list, all exports to Rhodesia, with minor exceptions which have been authorized by general permit, require the issuance of individual export licences. It is pursuant to this that the exports of oil and oil products were barred.
Today I have announced that in addition there are embargoes with regard to exports and imports which represent 100 per cent of our total trade both ways, so that we have now taken action to provide for a total embargo.
On the question of substance, namely as to whether the course we have followed is right, this government believes that the unity of the Commonwealth, our relations with African countries, and the evolutionary events in our time require the kind of action that all Commonwealth countries have taken, including Canada.
My hon. friend spoke earlier about the visit of the Queen to Canada. We all welcome and we all look forward to the visit of the Queen,
February 3, 1966

Supply-External Affairs the Queen of Canada; but let us not forget the events that occurred during the first week of December last, when African Commonwealth countries joined with other African countries in an ultimatum placed at the doorstep of the British government, to the effect that if more effective measures were not taken by Britain toward Rhodesia, these countries would withdraw their missions in London.
It was because of that situation that the conference of Prime Ministers took place in Lagos in the month of January, and the record will show that the government of Canada, realizing what this meant to the Commonwealth, urged certain countries, notably Tanzania and Ghana, and other countries that might have been considering withdrawing missions, to give serious consideration to the implications of such a step for Commonwealth unity, recognizing at the same time that these countries would not, by withdrawal of missions alone, thereby necessarily withdraw from the Commonwealth.
Therefore I am saying to my hon. friend- and I am not saying he is not sincere in the position he has taken today; I know he is -that it is a minority position. I am sure it is not one that is conducive to do what he would want, namely to promote the unity of the Commonwealth and afford this country and other countries like Britain, Australia and New Zealand, to join with the majority at the countries of the world in recognizing that we have faced up to certain necessary decisions. The international community cannot stand by when there is discrimination against people, merely on the ground of colour.
That is what is involved in this problem and that is why the government has taken the position it has. That is why I am asking this house, by the reaction it takes to these measures, to clearly indicate that the course we have taken in support of Britain and other Commonwealth countries, with the aid of countries outside the Commonwealth, was a course of wisdom, a course of courage and a course that represents a necessary development of our foreign policy.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question? Does the minister consider that the imposition of sanctions calculated to cause economic distress among both whites and coloured people in Southern Rhodesia is the type of kind Christian act that this country should adopt?
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that one would wish it had not been necessary to take such a course. I want to say to my hon. friend-and I do not like to put this on the basis of Christianity or any other form of religion-but on the basis of high morality, surely if one has to make a decision of this kind, there can be no doubt that the morality of the action we took will stand the test as compared to the kind of morality involved and the kind of discrimination that has been practised by governments in some countries of the world toward people who are not white.

Mr. Chairman, far be it from me to attempt to show the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) how to run his department, how to orient Canada's external affairs policy. I simply wish to add a few words by way of contribution and possibly, make a suggestion.
As a newcomer, I have listened closely to the remarks made in the course of this debate by the members of the various parties in the house, and I must say that, with a few exceptions, I have been very favourably impressed by the tone given at the onset of the debate. It has been understood that the issue here is, actually, the old biblical principle as to whether or not we are to be truly our brothers' keepers. In particular I admired the praiseworthy generosity and spontaneity with which the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) congratulated the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the excellent work he has done.
I was particularly struck also by the remarks made by an hon. member of the opposition, I think it was the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie). If I am not quite in order, Mr. Chairman, I hope you will let me know-but I hope we will get as soon as possible a list of the names of members with the number of their seat and the riding they represent, so that new members like myself can identify their colleagues.
As I was saying, I admired the high minded speech made by the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) who, although in the opposition, deemed it necessary to correct some impressions or opinions of his Conservative colleagues, in the name of sacred unity, a principle that binds us in the matter of international relations. But I feel I have to correct just the same a statement made by the hon. member when he said that he did not accept the point of view expressed this afternoon by
February 3, 1966	COMMONS
the hon. member tor Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) who stated that the province of Quebec should be able to sign cultural agreements, with France in particular, without prejudice to the federal jurisdiction. The argument of the hon. member for Sherbrooke struck me. He is a professor of constitutional Law. He knows what he is talking about. He backed up his statements with arguments which seemed very sound to me. Since the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) seems very sincere in his attitude, I would suggest that he meet a few times with the hon. member for Sherbrooke. I have the impression that it is only a misunderstanding between the hon. member for Sherbrooke and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Macquarrie) on that matter of cultural agreements that the province of Quebec can make with some countries, France in particular, under a formula which is perfectly acceptable to the officials of the Department of External Affairs and which in no way lessens their prestige or their authority.
I have been following for years now the progress of the external policy of my country and I find it most interesting. I told you I wanted to say a few words of congratulations: I think personally that the Leader of the Government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are a team particularly well prepared for the important mission they have to carry out as arbitrators in many a conflicts we have in this agitated and seething world, where so many countries might, at any moment, lose their bearings, if I may be allowed to lapse into the vernacular. I do not rely on my own opinion, but quoting a most convincing all-round viewpoint, expressed by some American and Canadian journalists whom I have been seeing for the last few months and who could observe at the United Nations or in Lagos on the occasion of European conferences either the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, journalists are not inclined to be enthusiastic over just anybody, but more than one told me on several occasions how proud they were to see the prestige enjoyed by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs with foreign diplomats, and the respect in which they are held. Their suggestions and proposals are often readily accepted by foreign diplomats.
I think it is important that this be said in the circumstances-because I am one of those who believe that if there is an area very
DEBATES	701
Supply-External Affairs important to the heightening of Canada's image and the securing of the widest possible influence in international relations, it is the area of External affairs. We should eliminate petty and destructive criticism and attempts should be made to keep the discussions on the high level maintained today by most members of this house.
That is at a highly constructive level. Quite properly, they were careful to avoid giving other nations who read reports of our discussions in the press, the notion that we might be divided on foreign policy in a way that could eventually be disastrous to our influence.
I also enjoyed the speeches of those who loudly proclaimed that we should be bound to our allies in the confrontation of these two worlds, and to those who share our ideals and understand the duties of solidarity. Occasionally constructive suggestions may be submitted. It is normal. But in most cases substantially, constantly and definitely, we should close ranks to avoid defeat by the communist ideology striving to absorb nations too weak to fight off this nefarious influence.
Mr. Chairman, this is the suggestion I should like to make to the house. In the field of external affairs, members must always show constant concern for the sacred union, to maintain Canada's image as large and as bright as possible, and make it larger still, so that Canada may increase her influence for peace and assist in the progress of nations which expect a lot from us and look to us with hope, as we all know.

Mr. Chairman, I should also like to make a contribution, but a very brief one, to this debate on external affairs.
view of the fact that time is fast going by, I shall be dealing tonight with only one question, and that is the presence in the United Nations of a score of French language African countries.
In 1960, when I was a delegate to the United Nations, I had been given special responsibility by the Minister of External Affairs of the day (Mr. Green) for establishing contacts with these new French speaking nations.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that Canada is a power that is respected by those young countries. Canada, because of its bi-ethnic character, because also of its cultural duality, has a very special role to play within this group of African states.
These African countries have full confidence in all our possibilities because in their
February 3, 1966

Supply-External Affairs eyes Canada is a country without territorial ambition and without a colonial past, and because we are in a good position to give these countries the benefit of our experience and of our knowledge in all fields.
The Canadian delegation to the United Nations must therefore multiply its efforts and representations so as to consolidate our friendship with these groups of young African countries. To this end, I would ask the minister to instruct our delegation to the United Nations to co-operate very closely with the countries of French Africa in various committees of the General Assembly and especially in the Fourth Commission where the problems of trusteeship are discussed.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Now, I know that at the present time we are very well represented in the Canadian delegation at the United Nations by the presence there of His Excellency the ambassador Paul Tremblay, whom we took the initiative of appointing to that post. I should also like to underline, because we used to work together, the dedication and effort shown by the present Under Secretary of State in 1961, when he headed the United Nations' legal committee. But those efforts and this work must be maintained and increased. Therefore, during the sessions of the General Assembly, the government should send a French speaking member as a delegate because, as I said, the General Assembly being made up as it is, it is essential to Canada's prestige and good reputation that French Canada be represented.
But our efforts and our foreign policy cannot be solely satisfied with establishing contacts with French speaking countries in Africa. Moreover, we must elaborate with respect to these countries a clearly defined policy in every field.
These young countries, Mr. Chairman, are at present undergoing economic development, in spite of the difficulties we know they are experiencing. Their political evolution is rather slow: to wit, the bloody revolutions of recent months.
It is undeniable that these countries are sadly lacking at the management level. They also need, to head their institutions, a greater number of men who are better qualified and more competent. Their natural resources have barely been tapped and even today, experts are called upon to develop them who often belonged to the former government or who come from the countries

which colonized them. Because there are strangers among their politicians, the young people of Africa are starting to doubt the independent status of their countries. This situation gives rise to unrest among the masses, as we have seen but recently.
It is of course obvious, Mr. Chairman, that those African countries may not have been quite ripe for independence. But in Africa, as elsewhere, complete political independence can never be achieved without economic independence.
It is in this sphere that Canada, on account of her bi-ethnical character, has a very special part to play in those French speaking countries. Until now, I do not think that our country has responded adequately to the appeal made by those countries. Here is what I believe the government should do, and without delay: First, contribute to the professional training of the young African people by offering more scholarships, so as to enable those students to attend Canadian universities. The government should also provide those countries with experts and technicians to help them in the development of their natural resources and also to enable them to strike an economic balance in their institutions.
I think also that the government should post commercial agents to these various countries in order that ours might take advantage of the many markets that are being organized in Africa at the present time.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, our government should appoint French speaking ambassadors in important French speaking African countries with a view to the establishment of economic ties and cultural relations through which all Canadians no doubt might be enriched.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL-QUEBEC-LISTING OF PROJECTS UNDERTAKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago most Quebec federal members received from the secretariat of that province a publication entitled "Quebec's Centennial Projects". Projects planned and to be carried out under the Nation's Centennial Act are well illustrated and include explanatory notes.
The presentation is in very good taste and gives an idea of the large commemorative buildings by which Quebec will mark the Centennial of Confederation. However, many have noticed and deplored the fact that the federal government's contribution is not too clearly indicated. It seems that, for every project, Ottawa's contribution-several million dollars-has not been made crystal clear.
It is true that in each case, the total cost, Quebec's share, the Centennial's share, and that of the promoter, as the case may be, are mentioned. The use of the word "centennial" to define Ottawa's contribution can easily cause some misunderstanding, more especially as in the first pages, reference is made to a centennial committee established by the Quebec government and made up solely of provincial representatives.
I might be urged to read the introductory notes and the legislative provisions appearing at the beginning of the pamphlet and not to impute motives unfairly. I agree, but I suggest that it would have been easy to be more specific, so as not to minimize the contribution of the federal government.
I have in hand, Mr. Speaker, the introductory notes as well as the legislative provisions and looking upon these two pages I realize that for the Quebec conservatory of which I shall speak later, the Ottawa and the Quebec governments will each contribute an appreciable amount. But in the other explanations, a centennial committee is mentioned which was created by the province of Quebec, and it is said that the province will co-operate with the Centennial Commission through the provincial secretary's office but nothing is said about the total federal government's contribution.
In the legislative provisions, reference is made to an act adopted by the province of Quebec. In the implementation of the act, co-operation is mentioned time and time again.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
One wonders, in glancing at this text, whether the province of Quebec has not, once again, preferred the opting out formula, all the more so that later on they even succeed in saying that to all those projects the province of Quebec, for its part, contributes $1 million more than the centennial commission.
I do not want to talk any longer about all these details, but it seems to me that a little more effort could have been made to further define our contribution.
All the more because it is obvious that in some counties, members of the provincial legislature have sought for themselves all the credit and publicity for those centennial projects. In the county of Beauharnois, among others, where the project comes under the responsibility of a private corporation, the member went all out so that there would be no reference to the federal government and even less to the municipal level of government. He sought to give instructions to the local committee in fields that were none of his business and even threatened to block the project if things did not go as he wanted them to. As for us, it is true that we do not have a member just like the others. But I know that other members of Parliament have had cause to complain of the lack of cooperation between the two levels of government.
Some will be under the impression that Quebec is always trying to monopolize the headlines and to take all the credit.
Mr. Speaker, how is it that federal representatives are more often than not treated like poor relations when joint projects are inaugurated? How is it that no federal representative was officially invited when the first shovelful of earth was turned up to mark the beginning of the construction work on the Quebec conservatory? Is not Ottawa contributing a sum of $2,800,000 to this centennial project in the capital of Quebec?
It is true that nowadays the onus is left to Ottawa and it seems quite fair to say that, if things are going badly, it is Ottawa's fault, but when things are going well, it is because of Quebec.
The purpose of my question to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) is not to start a controversy, but rather to underline a situation that could easily be remedied and to achieve thereby a better understanding and co-operation, especially on the eve of the centennial of confederation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: CANADIAN CENTENNIAL-QUEBEC-LISTING OF PROJECTS UNDERTAKEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry, I think I should begin by referring to the publicity to be given to centennial projects, especially those undertaken under agreements with the ten provincial governments.
Those agreements include two clauses concerning the matter of advertising, but which make no provision for printed matter, whether releases, tracts or pamphlets, such as those mentioned by the hon. member. All they stipulate is that the contribution of both governments be mentioned on signs erected on the building sites, as well as on the permanent plaques and signs affixed as an indication of sponsorship.
Although it is not provided for in writing under the agreements mentioned, printed advertising has nevertheless been the subject of an unofficial agreement between the federal centennial commission and the proper provincial bodies. They have agreed that in all printed matter, appropriate mention will be made of the contribution of each government.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I may admit that the federal centennial commission is not entirely satisfied with the publicity given to the role it must play in these various projects. That is a general complaint not limited to any single province. Although I have not enough time to get into details tonight, I may say that the centennial commission is now taking action to correct the situation as far as possible.
A basic problem arises here, however, because to a certain extent, the federal commission is the last, among the parties concerned, to see the various projects in question and, consequently, cannot take part in the publicity given to any of the projects at certain initial stages. Any municipality, for instance, may announce its own decision as to the projects it intends to submit to the province. If the federal centennial commission sought to take part in the publicity at that stage, it would prejudge how the project would be received even before it had been officially submitted to the federal government for approval and financial contribution. It is the same thing at the next stage.
Again, at the second stage, the federal centennial commission is not in a position to announce the project, since it has not had the opportunity to decide about the project officially.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON DAIRY POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I raised a very important matter which concerns all the members who represent rural areas. This matter and the way it will be treated, will determine the future of the dairy producers of Canada.
We know that this government will have to find means of providing a minimum price of $4 per hundredweight for industrial milk and this, at the very beginning of the next dairy year, that is next April 1.
To this end, the government has announced the following in the Speech from the Throne and I quote:
Legislation to establish a Canadian Dairy Commission will be placed before you.
Hon. members do not know yet the main points of that project; they are not yet sure if that new dairy policy which will be announced shortly will reach the minimum goal of $4 per hundredweight of industrial milk asked for by all dairy farmers in Canada. Let me tell you right away that this goal is reasonable and that we, on this side of the house, support it.
I would like to quote many speeches made during the election campaign, and the stands we took on that matter, views which we will fight for to the bitter end. That policy to pay $4 per hundredweight, we want to know what it is today, or as soon as possible.
If the minister intends to submit that resolution to the house shortly, I feel that it should also be studied in committee.
February 3, 1966
The minister should make it a point to explain the general purpose of such a bill to the committee if it is to make suggestions to him.
Moreover, I would ask the minister to submit to the committee the new dairy policy to be announced shortly, and here is why. This would not only afford him the opportunity of ascertaining the views of the members representing the various sections of the country but also help him to prepare the best possible bill, not for one but for many years to come.
This would also enable the committee to study the new dairy policy coming into force next April 1. I think the minister should accept this suggestion immediately, for he would thus have the co-operation of all the hon. members and the farm associations of the country.

If that is not so, then whoever wrote out the wording of the rule does not know much about the English language. And I hope it was not the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Certainly, if that is not the meaning of that clause, there are a series of redundant words in it. However, that is beside the point. In my opinion the meaning of the section should be worded much more clearly, and I would be pleased to discuss it with my hon. friend, to determine the meaning of the rules.
In regard to the question of the national dairy commission, and the dairy policy for the ensuing year, I would point out first of all to my hon. friend that we are discussing here the average price for manufacturing milk across Canada. In the previous year, before we came to office when the government of his party was in office, that was something like $2.84 per hundred. During this current year the average price, through policies that this government has instituted, in-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion eluding the supplementary payments and the deficiency policy, is at a national average of $3.50.
I would point out that this very appreciable improvement has been brought about in the short time we were in office, through the good policies of this government, which have, I think, appreciably improved the position of the farmer and of the producer of manufacturing milk.
I agree with my hon. friend that we have to do even better, and that is what we intend to do. I would point out also to my hon. friend that there have been discussions and negotiations with the provinces which have been directed to the end that there will be a national dairy policy. That policy is one that dairy people have been advocating for many, many years.
During the past year the province of Ontario has passed a Dairy Products Marketing Act, and I am very happy to relate, as the Minister of Agriculture for Ontario Hon. W. A. Stewart, recently stated, that this act was drawn in conjuction with, in co-operation with and after discussions with our federal officials, to make sure that the legislation would fit in with the principles and with the objectives of a national dairy commission.
I am also very happy to see that the province of Quebec from which my friend hails has announced in its Throne Speech that it too will pass legislation which will create a provincial milk marketing board. This will permit the setting of prices now in the province of Quebec, as well as in the province of Ontario which, in conjuction with federal policies, will enable a better price to be obtained for the manufacturing milk.
I can assure my hon. friend that to the best of my ability I am going to push the question of the national dairy policy and the national dairy commission. I hope that I will have the co-operation of my hon. friends opposite in this regard, and in respect of the national dairy policy of this year, which comes into effect on April 1, so that we will have that policy before this house in good time to give adequate and ample notice to all our farmers, that they may in turn make their own decisions in regard to production this year.
I will be very happy to take into consideration my hon. friend's suggestion that this matter be discussed by the agriculture committee of this house.
